section: Chapter 9: Operations — How Storage Systems Are Updated, Upgraded, and Migrated
title: Building takes years. Running a storage system takes decades
body: Day-2 operations means everything that happens to a storage system after launch. Over its decades-long life, every disk will be replaced, every server rebooted many times, the software upgraded thousands of times, the on-disk format changed, and eventually all the data moved to a completely new system. Through all of it, users still expect zero downtime and zero data loss. That makes operations, not the initial build, the part of storage engineering that lasts longest and carries the most risk.
deeper:
The chapter walks through how large companies handle day-2 work: automated repair of failed disks, fleet-wide firmware and software updates, safe config changes, online schema changes, storage engine swaps, and large data migrations. It draws on real stories from Meta, Dropbox, Uber, Discord, GitHub, Stripe, LinkedIn, AWS, and Google.

The framing matters because launch day is a snapshot. A system that looks perfect at launch still has to survive thousands of binary releases, kernel patches, drive swaps, and at least one full migration off itself. Each of those is a moment when the system is running in an unusual state: mixed versions, reduced redundancy, or data in two places at once. The rest of the chapter is basically a catalogue of techniques for keeping those unusual states safe: redundancy budgets, staged rollouts, cells, canaries, dual writes, and rollback paths. If you remember one idea, it is that every operation is itself a risk to durability and availability, and must be designed as carefully as the data path.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter call operations, not the initial build, the hard part of storage?
quiz.a: The system runs for decades, and during that time every disk, server, software version, and format changes, and data eventually moves elsewhere, all while users expect zero downtime and zero data loss.

section: 9.1 Why operations is the hard part
title: 13 dead drives a day: failure is a background process
body: Backblaze reported an annualized failure rate (AFR), the fraction of drives expected to fail per year, of 1.57 percent across 301,120 data drives in 2024. That works out to roughly 4,700 failed drives per year in one fleet, or about 13 every day. A hyperscaler with millions of drives replaces hundreds daily. At this scale a disk failure is not an incident to investigate. It is a constant background process the system must absorb automatically, without humans and without users noticing.
deeper:
This is the first of three facts that drive the whole chapter. The arithmetic is simple: fleet size times AFR gives failures per year, and dividing by 365 gives failures per day. The chapter's quiz uses the same math: 300,000 drives at 1.5 percent AFR is about 4,500 failures per year, about 12 per day.

The consequences show up everywhere later. Repair must be automated because there is always some data degraded somewhere. Paging a human per disk would burn out on-call engineers, so disk failures go to automation plus a daily replacement ticket queue. Maintenance windows cannot assume a healthy fleet, because real failures keep happening during upgrades, which is why the redundancy budget for maintenance must leave room for them. And capacity planning has to include the drives that are always out of service waiting for a swap.

The mindset shift is important: at small scale, a failed disk is news. At fleet scale, zero failed disks today would be the news.

quiz.q: Why does a Backblaze-sized fleet treat disk failure as a background process rather than an incident?
quiz.a: At 1.57 percent AFR over about 300,000 drives, roughly 13 fail every day, so failures must be absorbed automatically, not investigated one by one.

section: 9.1 Why operations is the hard part
title: Upgrades outnumber failures 1,000 to 1
body: Meta's Shard Manager paper found that software upgrades happen about 1,000 times more often than unplanned failures. Every kernel patch, firmware update, and binary release restarts servers, and each restart briefly takes that server's data or leadership roles out of service. So the most common reason a storage server goes away is not a crash but a deliberate, planned change. A system that only handles crashes gracefully, and treats planned restarts as an afterthought, is optimizing for the rare case.
deeper:
This fact reshapes priorities. If restarts from upgrades are a thousand times more frequent than crashes, then making planned restarts invisible pays off far more than squeezing more out of crash recovery. That is why Meta built Shard Manager largely around graceful primary handoff during planned events: before a server restarts, its primary shards move to another replica, so clients never see a leader disappear abruptly.

Planned change also gives you something crashes do not: advance notice. The system knows which server is about to go away, so it can drain primaries, check that no other replica of the same data is currently offline, and only then proceed. Treating an upgrade like a planned failure is a recurring theme later in the chapter, for firmware updates, rolling upgrades, and rack decommissioning.

The flip side is that each of these frequent changes is also a chance to introduce a bug, which leads directly to the third fact: change causes most outages.

quiz.q: What design priority follows from upgrades being about 1,000 times more frequent than unplanned failures?
quiz.a: Make planned restarts invisible, for example through graceful leadership handoff and draining, since they are by far the most common reason servers leave service.

section: 9.1 Why operations is the hard part
title: Most outages start with someone pushing a change
body: Google's SRE workbook says that in Google's experience, a majority of incidents are triggered by binary or configuration pushes. The two most famous storage-adjacent outages of the last decade were operational commands: the AWS S3 outage of February 28, 2017, where a command with a wrong input removed more servers than intended, and the Meta outage of October 4, 2021, where a maintenance command took down the backbone and an audit tool bug failed to stop it. The central problem: changing a system constantly without breaking it.
deeper:
Put the three facts together and the shape of the problem is clear. Failures are constant, planned changes are about 1,000 times more common than failures, and changes cause most outages. So the biggest lever on reliability is not better hardware but safer change.

Both example outages share a pattern: a human-initiated tool executed a destructive operation at large scale, and nothing in the tool stopped it. In S3's case the input was wrong and the tool removed more capacity than intended. In Meta's case the maintenance command itself was the trigger and the safety check that should have blocked it had a bug. Neither was a hardware failure or a clever attack.

The rest of the chapter answers the question these outages raise with specific techniques: staged rollouts and canaries to detect bad changes early, cells to limit how much a bad change can hurt, guardrails in tools so a wrong input cannot remove too much capacity, and a strong preference for making destructive operations slow and reviewed. The S3 remediation in particular becomes a template the chapter returns to several times.

quiz.q: What do the S3 2017 and Meta 2021 outages have in common?
quiz.a: Both were triggered by operational commands, not hardware faults: a tool executed a destructive operation at scale and no guardrail stopped it (wrong input in S3, an audit tool bug at Meta).

section: 9.1 Why operations is the hard part
title: A design isn't done until you can upgrade, migrate, and roll back
body: Senior staff lens: a storage design is not finished until you can answer three questions. How do we upgrade it? How do we migrate off it? How do we roll back? Design reviews that skip these questions produce systems that are safe on launch day and dangerous a year later, when the first format change, fleet upgrade, or replacement system arrives and nobody planned for mixed versions, dual writes, or undoing a bad change.
deeper:
Each question maps to a concrete design property. Upgradeability means version compatibility in both directions, so old and new binaries can run side by side for days, and a controller that respects the durability budget while restarting servers. Migratability means data access goes through an abstraction layer, so a future backend swap changes one service instead of hundreds, and the data model does not depend on quirks only this store supports. Rollback means every step of every change can be undone, which in practice pushes teams toward two-phase format changes, feature flags, expand-and-contract schema changes, and keeping old systems receiving writes for a while after cutover.

These properties are cheap to build in at the start and very expensive to retrofit. A store with no abstraction layer in front of it, or an on-disk format that old code cannot read, can turn a routine upgrade into a year-long project. Asking the three questions in a design review is a cheap way to surface those problems while they can still be fixed on paper.

quiz.q: Why should a design review ask how to migrate off a storage system that is not even built yet?
quiz.a: Migration readiness (abstraction layers, compatible formats, rollback paths) is cheap to design in and very expensive to retrofit; skipping it makes the system dangerous a year later.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
title: The repair loop: from dead disk back to full redundancy
body: When a disk dies, some data loses one copy or one erasure-coded fragment. That data is now degraded: it has less redundancy than intended. Repair (also called re-replication, or reconstruction for erasure codes) restores full redundancy before more failures happen. The loop runs: detect the problem, quarantine the disk and stop new writes, identify affected chunks or placement groups, prioritize those with the fewest remaining copies, rebuild copies on other disks in valid failure domains, verify checksums and redundancy, then ticket a drive swap.
deeper:
The loop is simple to draw but each step hides a subtle decision. Detection is easy for a dead disk but hard for one that is slow or returns occasional errors. Quarantine has to balance wasting bandwidth on a disk that will come back against leaving data degraded. Identifying affected data requires accurate metadata mapping disks to chunks or placement groups. Prioritization means not all degraded data is equally urgent. Rebuilding must obey the same failure-domain placement rules as the original copies (Chapter 8), so a replacement cannot land in the same rack as a surviving copy. Verification with checksums confirms the new copies are actually correct rather than faithfully duplicated corruption.

The final step is physical: a ticket asks a technician to swap the drive and return the slot to the pool. Notice the ordering. Data safety is restored by software across the cluster long before anyone touches the dead drive. The drive swap is a capacity concern, not a durability emergency, which is why it can be batched into a daily ticket queue.

quiz.q: Why can the physical drive swap wait for a routine ticket queue?
quiz.a: Software rebuilds the lost copies on other disks first, restoring full redundancy; the swap only restores capacity, not durability.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
title: Dead disks are easy. Slow disks are the real trouble
body: The detection step of repair watches for disk errors, missed heartbeats, and SMART alerts. A disk that is completely dead is easy to spot. A disk that is merely slow, or returns occasional errors, is much harder: it still answers, so it may never trip a simple health check, yet it can drag down every request that touches it. Many systems therefore treat a disk with rising latency as failing and drain it proactively, moving its data away before it fully dies.
deeper:
A slow disk is often worse than a dead one for users. A dead disk is removed and its reads go elsewhere. A slow disk stays in service, and because many storage reads fan out across several disks (for example, reading fragments of an erasure-coded stripe), one slow disk can make every read that includes it slow. Chapter 8's point about fan-out and tail latency applies directly: at high fan-out, the slowest participant decides the latency.

That is why later in the chapter observability calls for per-disk latency histograms rather than averages. An average across a node can look fine while one disk has a terrible tail. With histograms per disk you can find the one outlier and drain it.

Proactive draining is the natural response: treat rising latency or rising error counts as a signal of impending failure, and move data off while the disk still works. Draining a still-readable disk is cheaper and safer than reconstructing its data after it dies, because the data can be copied directly instead of rebuilt from other replicas or fragments.

quiz.q: Why might a slow disk hurt users more than a dead one?
quiz.a: A dead disk is removed and traffic goes elsewhere, but a slow disk stays in service and slows every fanned-out read that touches it.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
title: Why storage waits before repairing a vanished server
body: If a whole server reboots, its disks usually come back within minutes. Starting repair the instant it stops responding would copy huge amounts of data for nothing and compete with user traffic. So systems wait a short grace period before declaring the disks lost; Ceph, for example, waits before marking an OSD 'out'. The trade-off is real: every minute of waiting is a minute the data stays degraded, with less redundancy, and exposed to a second failure. After the grace period, risk-based priority takes over.
deeper:
The chapter's quiz frames this exactly: it is dangerous to repair immediately because most unresponsive servers come back after a reboot, so immediate repair wastes large amounts of bandwidth and may hurt user traffic. It is dangerous to wait too long because data sits with reduced redundancy and another failure could cause loss.

The scale of the waste is easy to underestimate. Using the chapter's own back-of-envelope, one server with 36 drives of 20 TB at about 70 percent full holds about 500 TB. Kicking off a full rebuild of 500 TB because a server took five minutes to reboot is an enormous, pointless load on the network and on every disk supplying source data.

In Ceph, an OSD (object storage daemon, roughly one per disk) that stops responding is first marked down, and only after a delay marked out, at which point its placement groups are remapped and recovery begins. The grace period is a tunable, and choosing it is a direct trade between bandwidth efficiency and time spent degraded. It pairs with prioritization: data already near its last copy should not wait as patiently as data missing just one.

quiz.q: What are the risks on each side of the repair grace period?
quiz.a: Too short wastes huge bandwidth rebuilding servers that come back after a reboot; too long leaves data degraded and exposed to a second failure causing loss.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
title: Rebuilt copies must still obey failure-domain rules
body: When repair creates a replacement copy or fragment, it cannot put it just anywhere with free space. The new copy must respect the same failure-domain rules as the originals: copies of the same data must live in different racks, power domains, or other units that fail together (Chapter 8). So you cannot place the replacement copy in the same rack as a surviving copy. Breaking this rule during repair quietly creates data that looks fully redundant but could be lost to a single rack failure.
deeper:
This is a subtle source of latent risk. A naive repair scheduler optimizing for speed would pick whatever target disk is emptiest or closest to the source. The copy count goes back to three and all dashboards turn green, but two of those copies might now share a rack, so one top-of-rack switch failure or power event takes out both. The system has restored redundancy on paper while reducing it in reality.

The same constraint applies to erasure-coded stripes: each fragment of a stripe should sit in a distinct failure domain so the stripe survives as many domain losses as it has parity. Repair has to find a target that keeps that property.

Placement rules also interact with repair speed. The chapter later explains that spreading each disk's data across many other disks, rather than pairing it with a fixed mirror partner, lets rebuild run in parallel across many sources and targets. Failure-domain constraints limit which of those targets are eligible, so the placement algorithm has to satisfy both goals at once. Later, config changes to placement rules are called out as needing automated invariant checks for exactly this reason.

quiz.q: How could a fast repair restore copy count yet reduce real durability?
quiz.a: By placing the new copy in the same rack as a surviving copy, so one rack failure can now destroy both despite the count looking healthy.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
title: Rebuilding a 500 TB server: 6 days or 14 hours
body: Repair bandwidth is the network and disk throughput spent rebuilding lost data, and it competes with user traffic. The chapter's back-of-envelope: a server with 36 drives of 20 TB, about 70 percent full, holds about 500 TB. If it dies permanently and the cluster rebuilds at 1 GB/s total, that takes about 500,000 seconds, almost 6 days. At 10 GB/s it takes about 14 hours. The wider the rebuild is spread across many disks, the faster it finishes.
deeper:
The numbers matter because the rebuild window is the window of vulnerability. During those 6 days, every chunk that had a copy on the dead server is running with one fewer copy, and a second or third failure in that window could cause data loss. Cutting the window from 6 days to 14 hours cuts exposure roughly tenfold.

How do you get 10 GB/s? Not from one disk: a single drive can only write so fast. You get it by parallelism. If the dead server's data is spread across hundreds of other disks, then hundreds of sources can each send a slice and hundreds of targets can each receive a slice at the same time. This is one reason placement spreads each disk's data across many other disks rather than assigning it a fixed mirror partner. With a fixed partner, the whole rebuild funnels through one surviving disk and one new disk, which is slow and hammers them.

The trade-off is that faster repair takes bandwidth from users. That tension is why the chapter recommends scaling repair speed with risk rather than picking one fixed rate.

quiz.q: Why does spreading each disk's data across many other disks speed up repair?
quiz.a: Many source and target disks can rebuild slices in parallel, instead of funnelling the whole rebuild through one fixed mirror partner.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
title: Erasure coding's hidden tax: 10x repair traffic
body: Erasure coding saves space compared with replication, but makes repair more expensive. With RS(10,4), a Reed-Solomon code that splits data into 10 data fragments plus 4 parity fragments, rebuilding one lost fragment requires reading 10 other fragments and decoding. So repair network traffic is about 10 times the amount of data lost. With 3-way replication, you simply copy from one surviving replica. This is why Azure Storage uses LRC (local reconstruction codes), which reduce the number of reads needed for repair.
deeper:
The chapter's quiz asks exactly this: RS(10,4) repair uses more bandwidth because rebuilding one fragment needs 10 surviving fragments read and decoded, while replication copies from one surviving replica. For the same amount of lost data, EC repair reads about 10x.

Combine this with the previous back-of-envelope. If a 500 TB server's data is erasure-coded with RS(10,4), rebuilding it means reading on the order of 5 PB across the cluster, not 500 TB. That either makes repair take much longer or eats much more of the network, and both hurt. It also means EC clusters feel repair traffic much more acutely when many disks fail together, such as a rack loss.

LRC, covered in Chapter 1, adds local parity fragments computed over smaller groups of data fragments. A single lost fragment can then be rebuilt from its small local group instead of the full stripe, cutting repair reads substantially. Azure Storage adopted it for exactly this operational reason. The general lesson: when you choose a redundancy scheme, you are also choosing your repair cost, and repair cost is an operations problem you will pay every single day.

quiz.q: Why does RS(10,4) repair use more network bandwidth than 3-way replication for the same lost data?
quiz.a: Rebuilding one fragment requires reading 10 surviving fragments and decoding, about 10x the lost data, while replication just copies one surviving replica.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
title: Repair the data closest to its last copy first
body: Not all degraded data is equally at risk. A 3-replica chunk with 2 copies left is less urgent than one with only 1 copy left. An RS(10,4) stripe missing 3 fragments is one failure away from the edge. Good repair schedulers keep a priority queue: the fewer remaining redundancy units a piece of data has, the higher its priority and the more bandwidth it may use. Ceph, for example, tracks the state of every placement group, such as degraded or undersized, so recovery can be ordered by risk.
deeper:
Think of redundancy units as the number of additional failures the data can survive. A chunk with 3 replicas and 2 left can survive one more failure; with 1 left it can survive none. An RS(10,4) stripe can lose 4 fragments, so with 3 missing it has one unit of margin left. Priority should follow that remaining margin, not the order in which failures were detected.

This matters most on bad days. When a rack fails, thousands of chunks may become degraded at once, most of them missing just one copy. If a second disk then fails during the rebuild, a small subset of chunks drop to their last copy. A first-in, first-out repair queue would leave those behind thousands of less urgent chunks. A risk-ordered queue jumps them to the front.

Ceph's placement group states make this practical: the system knows, for every placement group, whether it is fully clean, degraded, or undersized, and can schedule recovery accordingly. Priority also ties to bandwidth: high-risk repair should be allowed to use more of the cluster's throughput, even at some cost to user latency.

quiz.q: Why is FIFO a bad order for a repair queue?
quiz.a: It can leave data at its last copy stuck behind many chunks missing just one copy; ordering by remaining redundancy fixes the most at-risk data first.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
title: Throttling repair to one low rate turns bad days into data loss
body: Common mistake: throttling repair to a fixed low rate to protect user latency. On normal days this works nicely, because repair stays quiet and users never notice it. But on the day a rack fails and a second disk dies during the rebuild, the slow repair leaves data at its last copy for too long, and it turns into data loss. Repair speed should scale with risk: slow and gentle for 'one copy missing', fast and aggressive for 'last copy'.
deeper:
The mistake is tempting because its costs are invisible most of the time. Latency complaints are loud and immediate; data loss risk is silent until the one day it materializes. Teams tune repair against the loud signal and accidentally set up a failure for the silent one.

The back-of-envelope from the same section shows the stakes. At 1 GB/s a 500 TB rebuild takes almost 6 days. If a fixed throttle holds repair near that rate even after a second failure, some chunks may sit at their last copy for days. Allowing repair to jump to 10 GB/s for those chunks shrinks the window to hours.

The better design connects the priority queue to bandwidth. Data missing one unit of redundancy gets repaired politely in the background. Data at minimum redundancy gets repaired as fast as the cluster can manage, and a brief latency hit is accepted because the alternative is permanent loss. This is also why the observability section says the most important storage dashboard shows how many chunks are at their last unit of redundancy and how fast repair is going.

quiz.q: What goes wrong with a fixed low repair rate, and what should replace it?
quiz.a: When a second failure hits during rebuild, slow repair leaves data at its last copy too long and it can be lost; repair speed should scale with risk.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
title: SMART: the counters every drive reports about itself
body: SMART (Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology) is a set of counters that drives report about their own health: reallocated sectors, pending sectors, seek errors, temperature, and more. A reallocated sector is a bad spot the drive has remapped to a spare area. The appeal is obvious: if these counters predicted failure, operators could replace drives before they die, turning surprise failures into calm, planned swaps. It is tempting to build a drive-replacement strategy around SMART. The evidence says to be careful.
deeper:
SMART exists on essentially every hard drive, so it is free data. The counters track physical symptoms that intuitively sound like warning signs. Reallocated sectors mean the drive has already found and remapped bad areas. Pending sectors are areas the drive suspects are bad but has not yet remapped. Seek errors hint at mechanical trouble with the head positioning. Temperature is tracked because heat is widely believed to shorten drive life.

The temptation is to write a simple rule such as 'replace any drive with more than N reallocated sectors' and assume that failures will now be caught in advance. The next card covers Google's 2007 FAST study, which tested that belief on a large drive population and found it mostly does not hold for individual drives. The distinction to keep in mind is between a signal that is useful when it fires and a signal whose absence proves health. SMART turns out to be the first kind, not the second, which shapes how it should be used in a repair pipeline.

quiz.q: Why is SMART attractive for operations teams?
quiz.a: It is free per-drive health data, and if it predicted failures reliably, drives could be swapped before they die instead of after.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
title: Google's 2007 finding: most failed drives showed no SMART warning
body: Google's 2007 FAST study of a large drive population concluded that models based on SMART parameters alone are unlikely to be useful for predicting individual drive failures. Over 56 percent of failed drives had no counts in the four strongest SMART signals. Even using all SMART parameters, over 36 percent of failed drives had zero counts on every variable. The study also found temperature and activity much less correlated with failure than expected. Many drives simply die with a clean SMART record.
deeper:
The numbers deserve careful reading. The four strongest SMART signals, the counters most associated with failure, were silent for more than half of the drives that failed. Widening the net to every SMART parameter still left more than a third of failed drives with nothing at all to report. No threshold on those counters could have flagged them, because there was nothing to threshold.

The temperature finding is a surprise to many people. Heat and heavy activity are commonly assumed to kill drives, but in this population they were much less correlated with failure than expected. That undercuts intuitive rules like 'replace hot drives first'.

The study was published by Google researchers (Pinheiro, Weber, and Barroso) at FAST 2007, and it remains the standard reference on this question. The chapter's key takeaways restate the headline: over 36 percent of failed drives showed no SMART signal at all. The practical meaning is that any storage system relying on SMART prediction to avoid surprise failures will still get surprised, frequently.

quiz.q: What does Google's finding that over 36 percent of failed drives had zero SMART counts imply?
quiz.a: No SMART threshold can catch those failures, so SMART cannot be relied on to predict individual drive failures; surprise failures will keep happening.

section: 9.2 Disk failure handling and automated repair
title: Use SMART to drain early, never as proof of health
body: The practical lesson from the SMART research is asymmetric. When SMART counters or error logs fire, treat them as a signal to drain the drive early, moving its data away while it still works. But never assume that the absence of a signal means a drive is healthy, because many drives fail with no warning at all. The storage system must be designed to survive surprise failures anyway, through redundancy and fast, risk-prioritized repair, with SMART as a helpful bonus rather than a foundation.
deeper:
This is a good general pattern for noisy signals in operations. A signal can be valuable when positive even if it is useless when negative. SMART warnings do correlate with trouble for some drives, and draining those drives proactively is cheap: copying data from a still-readable disk is faster and gentler than reconstructing it from other replicas or erasure-coded fragments after the disk dies.

What you must not do is let SMART reduce your redundancy planning. A team that believed SMART caught most failures might lower replication, lengthen the repair grace period, or throttle repair more aggressively. The Google data says that belief is false, so those choices would increase real data loss risk.

The observability section later lists SMART counters, media errors, reallocated sectors, temperature, and per-disk latency histograms as device-level signals, with the stated purpose of early drain of failing or slow disks. That is exactly the right role: an input to proactive draining, alongside latency and error logs, not a guarantee.

quiz.q: How should a storage system use SMART signals?
quiz.a: Drain drives early when SMART or error logs fire, but never treat a clean SMART record as healthy; redundancy and repair must still handle surprise failures.

section: 9.3 Firmware and drive updates at fleet scale
title: Bad firmware can kill every drive of one model at once
body: Drives, SSDs, NICs, and BMCs (baseboard management controllers, the small computers that manage servers out of band) all run firmware. Firmware bugs can cause data corruption, performance collapse, or bricked devices. Updating millions of devices is risky for two reasons. A bad version can affect every drive of the same model at once, a correlated failure that spreading replicas across racks does not protect against if every rack uses that model. And some updates need a power cycle or server reboot.
deeper:
Most redundancy designs assume failures are independent: disks die one at a time for unrelated reasons, so spreading copies across racks makes simultaneous loss of all copies very unlikely. Firmware breaks that assumption. If one firmware version has a bug that corrupts data or bricks the drive under some condition, every drive running it is exposed to the same bug at roughly the same time. Rack diversity is irrelevant if all three racks holding your replicas use the same drive model on the same firmware.

The second problem, reboots and power cycles, means a firmware update is not just a file copy. Each updated server leaves service temporarily, removing its replicas and leadership roles for that time. Across a fleet, that is a large amount of planned unavailability that has to fit within the system's redundancy budget while real failures continue in the background.

The next card covers the standard practices operators use to manage both risks: diversity, staged rollout, draining before update, and respecting the redundancy budget.

quiz.q: Why doesn't spreading replicas across racks protect against a firmware bug?
quiz.a: If all racks use the same drive model and firmware, the bug hits every copy at once; it is a correlated failure that rack diversity does not break.

section: 9.3 Firmware and drive updates at fleet scale
title: Firmware safety: diverse models, staged rollouts
body: Two standard practices guard against correlated firmware failures. First, diversity: when possible, avoid putting all replicas of a chunk on the same drive model or the same firmware version, so one bad version cannot hit every copy. Second, staged rollout: update a few drives, then a few servers, then a rack, then a cluster, watching error rates and latency at each step before going further. A bug caught at the few-drives stage costs almost nothing; the same bug found fleet-wide is a disaster.
deeper:
These practices are widely used and described in general terms by many operators rather than tied to one company's paper.

Diversity extends the failure-domain idea from physical location to hardware and software identity. Placement can treat drive model and firmware version as additional dimensions to spread across, just like rack and power domain. It is not always possible, because a fleet may be dominated by one model bought in bulk, which is why the chapter says 'when possible'. Even partial diversity helps: if a chunk's copies span two firmware versions, a bug in one leaves the other copy intact.

Staged rollout is the firmware version of canarying. Each stage is a checkpoint where error rates and latency are compared against the rest of the fleet. The stages grow in size so that confidence grows before exposure does. The same idea appears later for software rollouts as waves across cells and regions, with bake time between waves and automatic rollback. Firmware adds a wrinkle: some bugs only surface under particular workloads or after time, so bake time at each stage matters, not just a quick health check.

quiz.q: How do diversity and staged rollout each reduce firmware risk?
quiz.a: Diversity keeps one bad version from hitting all copies of a chunk; staged rollout detects a bad version while it affects only a few drives, before fleet-wide exposure.

section: 9.3 Firmware and drive updates at fleet scale
title: Treat every update as a planned failure, within budget
body: Two more firmware practices. Drain before update: treat the update like a planned failure, moving primaries away, updating, verifying, then returning the device to service. And respect the redundancy budget: never update more servers at once than the system can lose while still meeting its durability target. If a stripe survives 4 losses, you might allow at most 1 to 2 of its fragments to be offline for maintenance, keeping the rest of the budget for real failures that will keep happening meanwhile.
deeper:
Draining turns a potentially disruptive restart into a non-event for clients. If a server holds shard primaries or leader roles, moving them to other replicas first means no client request ever lands on a server mid-reboot. After the update, verification (the device came back, firmware version is right, error rates are normal) happens before it takes traffic again.

The redundancy budget is the more subtle idea. Redundancy exists to absorb failures. Maintenance spends some of it deliberately: while a server is offline for an update, every stripe with a fragment on it has one less unit of margin. Because unplanned failures continue at their usual background rate during maintenance (about 13 per day in a Backblaze-sized fleet), you must not spend the whole budget on planned work. With RS(10,4), which tolerates 4 lost fragments, taking at most 1 to 2 offline for maintenance leaves 2 to 3 units for real failures.

The same budget reappears in rolling software upgrades, where the upgrade controller must not restart two servers holding copies of the same data at once.

quiz.q: If a stripe tolerates 4 losses, why allow only 1 to 2 fragments offline for maintenance?
quiz.a: Unplanned failures keep happening during maintenance, so part of the redundancy budget must be reserved for them rather than spent on planned downtime.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
title: Rolling upgrades: old and new code must read each other
body: A rolling upgrade restarts servers a few at a time on the new version while the rest keep serving. For storage, a key requirement is version compatibility. During the upgrade, old and new versions run side by side, sometimes for days. New code must read data and messages written by old code (backward compatibility), and, so that you can roll back, old code must read what new code wrote (forward compatibility). Without both directions, either the upgrade breaks mid-way or rollback becomes impossible.
deeper:
Storage makes this harder than stateless services because data outlives the binary that wrote it. A stateless web server can be replaced and its old version forgotten. A storage server writes bytes to disk and messages to replicas, and those bytes will be read by whatever version is running later, possibly an older one after a rollback.

Consider a new version that writes records in a new format. If an old-version replica receives a replication message in that format and cannot parse it, the mixed-version cluster breaks during the upgrade. If the new version has a bug and you roll back, the old binary finds data on disk it cannot read, and rollback fails exactly when you need it.

The mixed period can last days because large fleets are upgraded in waves with bake time in between. So compatibility is not a brief edge case; it is the normal state of the system for a significant part of its life. The chapter's key takeaways list version compatibility in both directions as the first requirement for zero-downtime upgrades, alongside graceful leader handoff and a redundancy budget.

quiz.q: Why does a storage rolling upgrade need forward compatibility, not just backward?
quiz.a: For rollback: if the new version misbehaves, the old binary must be able to read data and messages the new version already wrote.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
title: Move leadership away before you restart the leader
body: Graceful handoff is a core requirement of rolling upgrades. Before restarting a server that is a shard primary or a Raft leader (the replica that coordinates writes for its group), the upgrade process first moves that leadership to another replica. Clients then keep talking to a healthy leader and never see the abrupt loss of one mid-request. Meta's Shard Manager was designed largely for this purpose: graceful primary handoff during planned events like software upgrades, which Meta found are far more common than crashes.
deeper:
Without graceful handoff, restarting a leader looks like a crash to the rest of the system. Clients get errors or timeouts, the replicas must detect the leader is gone (often via missed heartbeats), then hold an election or failover, and only then resume writes. That gap may be seconds, and during a large rolling upgrade it happens to every leader in the fleet.

Graceful handoff replaces that with a coordinated transfer: the current leader stops accepting new writes, ensures a successor is caught up, hands over, and redirects clients. Since the system knows the restart is coming, it can do this with no failed requests at all.

Meta's Shard Manager paper (SOSP 2021) connects this to the '1,000 times more upgrades than failures' finding. If planned restarts dominate, then making planned restarts invisible is the highest-value reliability feature a shard management system can offer. The chapter's industry box summarizes the division of labor: cells limit damage, canaries detect bad changes, and graceful handoff makes the restarts themselves invisible.

quiz.q: What happens if you restart a Raft leader without graceful handoff?
quiz.a: It looks like a crash: clients see errors, replicas must detect the loss and elect a new leader, causing a write gap, repeated for every leader in the upgrade.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
title: Never restart two holders of the same data at once
body: Every restart during a rolling upgrade temporarily removes that server's replicas from service. This is the durability budget constraint: the upgrade controller must never restart two servers that hold copies of the same data at the same time. If it did, some data could drop to a single copy, or become unavailable, while those servers reboot. A good upgrade controller therefore understands data placement, not just server lists, and picks each batch of restarts so no piece of data loses too many copies at once.
deeper:
This is the same redundancy budget introduced for firmware updates, applied to software. A naive rolling upgrade might restart 5 percent of servers at a time, chosen alphabetically or by rack. That can easily include two servers that happen to share replicas of the same chunks, and if a real disk failure lands during that window, those chunks may lose their last copy.

A placement-aware controller asks, for each candidate batch: after these servers go down, does every chunk still have enough copies (or fragments) to meet its durability target, with margin left for unplanned failures? Only batches that pass get restarted. This is also why cells and failure domains help upgrades: if data is placed so each rack or cell can be taken down without violating redundancy, upgrade batches can follow those boundaries naturally.

The chapter's summary lists three pillars of zero-downtime upgrades: version compatibility in both directions, graceful leader handoff, and a redundancy budget for maintenance. This card is the third pillar.

quiz.q: Why must an upgrade controller know data placement, not just a list of servers?
quiz.a: To avoid restarting two servers holding copies of the same data at once, which could drop that data to one copy or make it unavailable.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
title: Ship the reader first, flip the writer later
body: A good pattern for format changes is feature flags plus two-phase rollout. Phase one: ship code that can read the new format but still writes the old one. Roll it out everywhere. Phase two: once every server runs that code, flip a feature flag, a runtime switch that needs no new deploy, to start writing the new format. Because every server could already read both formats before anything wrote the new one, rolling back the binary is safe at every step.
deeper:
Walk through the failure cases to see why this works. During phase one, nothing writes the new format, so if the new binary misbehaves you roll back and the old binary sees only old-format data. Safe. When the flag flips, every server can already read the new format, so there is no mixed-version moment where a server receives data it cannot parse. If the new format itself causes trouble, you flip the flag back and servers resume writing the old format, while still being able to read what was written in the new one.

The unsafe alternative, shipping one binary that both reads and writes the new format, fails in two ways. During the rolling upgrade, new servers write data that old servers cannot read. And if you roll back, old binaries face new-format data on disk.

The same shape shows up repeatedly in this chapter: expand-and-contract schema changes add a column before anything depends on it, and large data migrations dual-write before switching reads. In each case you separate 'able to handle the new thing' from 'producing the new thing', so every step stays reversible.

quiz.q: Why ship code that reads the new format before any code writes it?
quiz.a: So when writing starts, every server can already read it, and rolling back the binary or flag never leaves a server facing data it cannot parse.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
title: Canarying: a small, timed test against a control group
body: Google's SRE workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation. A small canary population runs the new version while a control population runs the old one. You compare their metrics, such as errors, latency, and CPU, to decide go or no-go. The comparison against a control matters: it separates real regressions from normal fluctuations like time-of-day traffic shifts. The workbook notes you do not need a large canary to detect critical problems.
deeper:
Why a control group rather than just watching the canary's metrics against yesterday's? Because traffic, load, and error rates change constantly for reasons unrelated to the change. Comparing canary and control at the same moment, under the same conditions, isolates the effect of the new version.

Sizing is a judgment call. The workbook says a small canary is enough to catch critical problems, since severe bugs show up quickly even in a small population. But the right size depends on traffic volume, time of day, and which metrics you rely on. A canary that receives very little traffic, or runs during a quiet period, may not exercise the code enough to reveal a problem.

'Time-limited' is also part of the definition: the canary runs for a set evaluation period, then either proceeds or is rolled back. The next card covers why storage canaries need special metrics and longer evaluation, because many storage bugs are slow and silent rather than loud. Later, the chapter describes shifting reads gradually during a data migration as canarying applied to data.

quiz.q: Why compare the canary against a control population instead of historical metrics?
quiz.a: Traffic and load fluctuate constantly; comparing canary and control at the same time under the same conditions isolates the change's real effect.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
title: Storage canaries must watch the slow, silent metrics
body: A storage bug can corrupt data silently for days before any request fails. So storage canaries cannot rely only on the usual request metrics like error rate and latency. They should also watch signals that move slowly: checksum mismatches, compaction backlog, disk space growth, and replication lag. These reveal problems such as data written incorrectly, a background process falling behind, or a leak in space usage, long before users see errors. A canary that looks green on requests may still be quietly damaging data.
deeper:
Each metric catches a different class of slow bug. Checksum mismatches indicate data read back does not match what was written, the most direct sign of corruption. Compaction backlog, relevant to LSM-tree engines, shows whether background merging keeps up; a new version that compacts less efficiently may look fine for hours and then stall writes or blow up read amplification days later. Disk space growth catches bugs that leak space, fail to delete, or write more than intended. Replication lag shows whether replicas keep up with the primary; a regression here erodes durability and failover readiness without failing any request.

The implication for canary design is bake time. A storage canary that runs for twenty minutes and checks only error rates would pass many dangerous changes. Storage rollouts typically bake longer at each wave, and compare these slow metrics between canary and control.

This fits the chapter's broader theme that durability problems are silent until data is gone, while availability problems are loud. Both canary analysis and observability dashboards need to deliberately look for the silent kind.

quiz.q: Why aren't error rate and latency enough to canary a storage change?
quiz.a: Storage bugs can corrupt data or accumulate backlog silently for days before any request fails; slow metrics like checksum mismatches and replication lag reveal them earlier.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
title: Cells: split the system so one failure hits 10 percent
body: The blast radius of a change is how many users it can hurt if it is bad. Storage systems shrink it with cells. AWS describes a cell-based architecture as multiple isolated instances of a workload, each called a cell, with a thin cell router in front that routes requests by a partition key such as customer ID. AWS's example: if a workload uses 10 cells to serve 100 requests, a failure in one cell leaves 90 percent of requests unaffected. Changes are deployed compartment by compartment.
deeper:
The key word is isolated. Each cell has its own servers, storage, and ideally its own dependencies, so a bug, overload, or bad config in one cell does not spread to others. The cell router is deliberately thin, since it is the one shared component and must be simple enough to rarely fail.

Cells change how deployments work. Instead of rolling a new version across one big fleet, you roll it cell by cell. The first cell is effectively a production canary with a hard wall around it: if the change is bad, at most one cell's customers are affected. The chapter's wave diagram shows this: one box in one cell, then one cell in one zone, then more cells in one region, then remaining regions one at a time.

The chapter's quiz explains why you want both canaries and cells. A canary is a small, time-limited deployment that detects whether a change is bad by comparing it to a control. A cell is an isolated slice that limits how many users a bad change or failure can hurt. Canaries catch problems early; cells contain the problems canaries miss.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a canary and a cell, and why want both?
quiz.a: A canary detects a bad change by comparison with a control; a cell is an isolated slice limiting how many users are hurt. Cells contain what canaries miss.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
title: Physalia: millions of tiny databases for EBS
body: AWS's EBS control plane store, Physalia, described at NSDI 2020, takes cells to an extreme. Instead of one big configuration database, it runs 'millions of tiny databases', each holding only the configuration keys a particular client needs. Each tiny database is placed using knowledge of the datacenter topology, so it is available where its client is. A hardware failure or a bad change therefore affects only a tiny slice of clients, rather than every volume that depends on the control plane.
deeper:
EBS (Elastic Block Store) provides network block volumes, and its control plane stores configuration that volumes need, for example to decide which replica is authoritative. If that configuration store were one large system, a failure or bad deployment in it could affect vast numbers of volumes at once.

Physalia inverts the usual scaling approach. Rather than building one big, highly available database, it builds many very small ones, each scoped to what one client needs. The blast radius of any single failure becomes the set of clients using that tiny database, which by design is small.

Topology-aware placement adds a second benefit. Because each tiny database is placed near the client that needs it, in terms of datacenter layout, a network partition that isolates part of the datacenter tends to keep a client together with its configuration. The client can still reach what it needs even while other parts of the datacenter are unreachable.

The chapter's industry box lists AWS (cells, Physalia 2020) alongside Google and Meta as treating deployment safety as a design property rather than an afterthought.

quiz.q: How does splitting a control plane into millions of tiny databases reduce risk?
quiz.a: Each holds only one client's configuration, so any failure or bad change affects a tiny slice, and topology-aware placement keeps it reachable by its client.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
title: What AWS changed after the S3 outage of 2017
body: After the S3 outage of February 28, 2017, where a command with a wrong input removed more servers than intended, AWS described its fixes. It changed the removal tool to remove capacity more slowly, with safeguards preventing capacity from going below a minimum. It audited other operational tools for similar risks. And it reprioritized partitioning the index subsystem into smaller cells, to reduce blast radius and speed recovery. Cells were the structural fix; slower tools with minimum-capacity guards were the immediate one.
deeper:
AWS's post also revealed a second lesson: the index and placement subsystems had not been fully restarted in the larger regions for many years, and restarting them took longer than expected. A system that never restarts accumulates state and growth that nobody has tested recovery against. When it finally had to restart from scratch, recovery was slow precisely because it had grown so large.

That is where smaller cells help twice. They limit how much capacity a single mistaken command can affect, and they make recovery faster because each cell is smaller to restart.

The tooling fixes are just as important and more immediately copyable. Removing capacity slowly gives humans and monitoring time to notice a mistake before it spreads. A hard floor on minimum capacity means even a wrong input cannot take the system below what it needs to function. The chapter returns to this remediation three more times: as a guardrail rule for config changes, as a warning for datacenter decommissioning, and in the senior staff lens as a template worth copying for any operational tool.

quiz.q: Why did the S3 index restart take longer than expected in 2017?
quiz.a: The index and placement subsystems had not been fully restarted in larger regions for many years, so recovery at their grown size was untested and slow.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
title: Deploy in waves: one box, one cell, one region, then the rest
body: A safe deployment pipeline moves a new build through widening waves. First one box in one cell. Then wave 1: one cell in one zone. After bake time, meaning waiting while watching metrics, if everything looks fine, wave 2 covers more cells in one region. After another bake, wave 3 rolls to the remaining regions, one at a time. At any bake checkpoint where metrics look wrong, the pipeline triggers automatic rollback. Exposure grows only as confidence grows.
deeper:
The structure combines the ideas of this section. Canarying supplies the evaluation at each step: compare the new version against the old on errors, latency, and, for storage, slow signals like checksum mismatches and replication lag. Cells supply the containment: each wave is bounded by cell, zone, and region boundaries, so a bad build that slips past one checkpoint still hurts a limited set of users. Regions one at a time means that even the final wave never exposes the whole world simultaneously.

Bake time is what makes the waves meaningful. Rushing through them provides little protection, because slow storage bugs need time to show. The chapter later applies this same principle to emergencies: the fast path should still be staged, only with shorter bake times, rather than skipping stages entirely.

Automatic rollback matters because humans are slow and, during incidents, tired. If a metric crosses a threshold during bake, the pipeline should revert without waiting for someone to notice and decide. The rollback itself is only safe if the version compatibility and two-phase format change practices were followed.

quiz.q: What does bake time between deployment waves protect against?
quiz.a: Bugs that take time to show, especially slow storage problems; it lets metrics reveal a bad build before it spreads to more cells and regions.

section: 9.4 Rolling software upgrades with zero downtime
title: Detect, contain, hide: deployment safety as design
body: In industry: AWS (cells, and Physalia in 2020), Google (canarying in its SRE workbook), and Meta (Shard Manager, 2021) all treat deployment safety as a design property, not a process bolted on later. The three techniques divide the work. Cells limit the damage any single change can do. Canaries detect a bad change early by comparing it with a control. Graceful handoff makes the restarts themselves invisible to clients. Together they let these companies change systems constantly without users noticing.
deeper:
Each technique covers a gap the others leave. Canaries alone are not enough, because some bugs are too rare or slow to show up in a small canary, and a change that passes the canary still reaches everyone. Cells alone are not enough, because without detection a bad change would roll from cell to cell until someone noticed. Graceful handoff addresses a different problem entirely: even a perfect build causes disruption if deploying it means abruptly killing leaders across the fleet.

Calling these design properties means they shape architecture. You cannot add cells to a system whose data and dependencies are all shared without major rework. You cannot do graceful handoff without a shard manager or consensus protocol that supports leadership transfer. You cannot do meaningful canarying without metrics comparable between canary and control populations.

This connects back to the senior staff lens at the start of the chapter: how do we upgrade it, migrate off it, and roll back? The companies in this box answered those questions at design time, which is why their constant changes rarely become outages.

quiz.q: Why aren't canaries alone enough for deployment safety?
quiz.a: Some bugs are too rare or slow to appear in a small canary; cells are needed to contain them, and graceful handoff to avoid disruption from restarts themselves.

section: 9.5 Config changes: the quiet killer
title: Config is 'just data' until it takes down the service
body: A config change alters system behavior without new code: a flag, a limit, a routing table, a placement rule, a quota. It feels safe because it is 'just data'. It is not. Google explicitly lists configuration pushes, next to binary pushes, as the main incident triggers. The Meta 2021 outage was a maintenance command, and the S3 2017 outage was a mistyped command parameter. A single wrong value can change how an entire fleet routes traffic or places data, instantly and everywhere.
deeper:
Config is dangerous for several reasons. It often skips the review, testing, and staged rollout that code gets, precisely because it seems harmless. It usually takes effect quickly, often fleet-wide, since the whole point is to change behavior without a redeploy. And it can be just as powerful as code: a placement rule decides where every replica lives, a quota decides who can write, and a routing table decides where every request goes.

The outages cited make the point concrete. In S3's case the input to an operational command was wrong, and the tool removed far more servers than intended. In Meta's case a maintenance command took down the backbone network. Neither involved a new binary; both involved an operator-supplied instruction executed at scale.

For storage specifically, config mistakes can hurt durability, not just availability. A bad placement rule might put multiple replicas in one rack; the system keeps working and looks healthy until that rack fails. The next cards list the rules experienced teams use to make config as safe as code.

quiz.q: Why is config often more dangerous than it looks?
quiz.a: It feels like harmless data so skips review and staging, yet it takes effect quickly and fleet-wide, and can change routing, placement, or capacity as powerfully as code.

section: 9.5 Config changes: the quiet killer
title: Treat config like code: reviewed, staged, reversible
body: Experienced storage teams apply three rules that give config the same safety as binaries. Config is code: it lives in version control, is reviewed, tested, and validated before rollout. Config goes through the same staged rollout as binaries: canary, cells, waves, with bake time between. And fast rollback: always keep the last known good config ready to push, so a bad change can be reverted in moments. These rules remove the illusion that config is a safe shortcut around the deployment pipeline.
deeper:
Version control gives you history (who changed what, when, and why) and makes the last known good config trivially retrievable. Review catches the typo or wrong number that the author missed. Testing and validation run the new config through checks before any production system sees it.

Staged rollout is arguably the most important rule. A config pushed to every server at once has an unlimited blast radius. The same config pushed to one cell first, then more cells, then regions, with metric comparison at each step, turns a potential global outage into a contained one. The chapter's key takeaways put it bluntly: config changes need the same pipeline as code.

Fast rollback matters because config problems often show up immediately. If the last known good version is ready to push, recovery is a single action rather than a scramble to figure out what the previous values were. This also depends on version control: you cannot quickly restore a state you never recorded.

The next card adds two more rules specific to operational tools and invariants: guardrails and program-checked validation.

quiz.q: Why should config use the same staged rollout as binaries?
quiz.a: A config pushed everywhere at once has unlimited blast radius; staging through canary, cells, and waves contains a bad value to a small slice first.

section: 9.5 Config changes: the quiet killer
title: Guardrails and invariants: let programs say no
body: Two more config rules. Guardrails in tools: a command that removes capacity must refuse to remove more than a safe fraction, and must move slowly, which is exactly the S3 remediation. Validate against invariants: express safety rules as properties a program checks before rollout, for example 'this placement rule leaves every stripe with at least N fragments in distinct racks'. Checked by a program, not by eye. Humans reviewing a config diff miss subtle violations; a validator checking every stripe does not.
deeper:
Guardrails move safety into the tool itself, so it does not depend on the operator typing the right value. A capacity-removal command with a hard ceiling on how much it will remove, and a slow execution rate, makes a wrong input survivable. Even if the operator asks to remove a whole region, the tool refuses or proceeds slowly enough for monitoring to catch it. AWS added exactly these safeguards after the 2017 S3 outage: remove capacity more slowly, never below minimum.

Invariant validation is about correctness that is too subtle to eyeball. A placement rule change might look reasonable in review but, combined with the current rack layout, leave some stripes with two fragments in the same rack. The only reliable way to know is to evaluate the rule against the actual topology and data layout and check every stripe. This is the same principle as decommissioning verification later in the chapter: use the actual metadata, not assumptions.

Both rules share a philosophy: when the cost of a mistake is huge, make the system refuse dangerous actions rather than trusting humans to avoid them.

quiz.q: Why validate a placement rule with a program instead of human review?
quiz.a: Subtle violations, like two fragments ending up in one rack given the actual topology, are nearly invisible in a diff; a program can check every stripe.

section: 9.5 Config changes: the quiet killer
title: Emergency pushes still need staging, just faster
body: Common mistake: allowing 'emergency' config pushes to skip the staged pipeline. It sounds reasonable, since during an incident you want the fix out immediately. But emergencies are exactly when people are tired, rushed, and most likely to make mistakes. A hasty fix pushed everywhere at once can turn one outage into a bigger one. The better design: make the fast path still staged, only with shorter bake times. You keep containment and detection, just compressed.
deeper:
The logic is about when errors are most likely. Under normal conditions, engineers are rested, changes are planned, and reviewers have time. During an incident, the person pushing the fix may have been awake for hours, is under pressure from stakeholders, and is working with incomplete information about the cause. That is when a typo or wrong assumption is most likely, and a pipeline bypass removes the very safeguards that would catch it.

Keeping the fast path staged means the emergency fix still goes to one cell first, still gets compared against metrics, and can still be rolled back automatically. Shorter bake times make it fast enough for an emergency. The cost is a few extra minutes; the benefit is that a wrong fix only damages one cell instead of everything.

This links to the chapter's automation rule: anything irreversible should be slow and guarded. Emergency pushes feel like a special case, but the consequences of a bad push are no less serious because the situation is urgent, so the guardrails should not disappear either.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't emergency config pushes bypass staged rollout?
quiz.a: Emergencies are when people are tired and rushed, so mistakes are likeliest; staging with shorter bake times keeps containment while staying fast.

section: 9.6 Schema and format changes in databases
title: A plain ALTER TABLE can lock a big table for hours
body: In MySQL, a plain ALTER TABLE on a large table can lock the table or rebuild it for hours. It can also cause long replication lag, because replicas must replay the same heavy operation. For something like a 1 TB table serving user profiles, hours of blocked writes or badly lagging replicas are not acceptable. Online schema change (OSC) tools solve this by performing the change without holding the original table hostage, letting the application keep reading and writing throughout.
deeper:
The problem scales with table size. On a small table, ALTER TABLE finishes in moments and nobody notices. On a 1 TB table, rebuilding every row takes a long time, and depending on the operation and MySQL version, writes may be blocked for much of it. Even when the primary handles it acceptably, replicas apply the change after the primary finishes, and while they grind through the rebuild they fall behind on all other replication traffic. Lagging replicas mean stale reads and reduced failover safety.

Schema changes are also frequent in a living product: new features need new columns, performance work needs new indexes. A team that can only change large tables during scheduled downtime will either stall its product or accept outages.

OSC tools, covered next, get around this by copying into a new table in the background, keeping it in sync with ongoing writes, and swapping it in at the end. Spanner takes another route by building schema changes into the database itself. Either way, the goal is the same: the table keeps serving throughout the change.

quiz.q: Why does ALTER TABLE on a big MySQL table also hurt replicas?
quiz.a: Replicas replay the same heavy rebuild after the primary, falling far behind on other replication traffic, causing stale reads and weaker failover.

section: 9.6 Schema and format changes in databases
title: Online schema change: build a ghost table, then swap
body: All popular online schema change tools follow the same five steps. First, create an empty ghost table (also called a shadow table) with the new schema. Second, copy rows from the original table in small batches. Third, capture ongoing changes to the original and apply them to the ghost table. Fourth, throttle when replicas lag or load is high. Fifth, cut over: atomically rename the ghost table to replace the original. The application keeps using the original table until the instant of the swap.
deeper:
Each step addresses a specific risk. Small-batch copying avoids the long locks of a single giant operation; each batch is quick, so normal traffic interleaves with it. Change capture solves the problem that the original table keeps receiving inserts, updates, and deletes during a copy that may take hours; without it the ghost table would be stale by the time copying finished. Throttling protects production: if replicas start lagging or the primary is overloaded, the tool slows down or pauses so the migration never becomes the cause of an incident.

The atomic rename at cut-over is what makes the switch invisible. At one instant, the table name points to the old structure; at the next, it points to the new one with all data and recent changes applied. The application does not need to know a migration happened.

The tools differ mainly in step three, how they capture ongoing changes. Some use triggers on the original table; others read MySQL's binary log. That choice has large operational consequences, covered on the next cards. The chapter's key takeaways summarize the pattern: copy into a ghost table, capture changes, throttle, and cut over.

quiz.q: Why must an online schema change tool capture ongoing changes during the copy?
quiz.a: The original table keeps receiving writes during an hours-long copy; without capturing and applying them, the ghost table would be stale at cut-over.

section: 9.6 Schema and format changes in databases
title: Trigger-based OSC: simple, but it taxes every write
body: Some online schema change tools capture ongoing changes with triggers: database hooks on the original table that fire on every insert, update, or delete and copy that change into the ghost table. Percona's pt-online-schema-change works this way, as does Meta's OSC, Meta's open-sourced tool for MySQL. The approach is simple. But triggers add load to every write on the original table, and because they are part of each write, they cannot be truly paused while the migration is throttled.
deeper:
Triggers are attractive because the database does the change capture for you: install a trigger, and every modification to the original is mirrored into the ghost table as part of the same statement. No external process needs to parse logs.

The cost is that every application write now does extra work: the original write plus the trigger's write to the ghost table. On a busy table, that overhead is significant, and it exists for the entire duration of the migration, which may be many hours.

The pausing problem is subtle but important. OSC tools throttle when replicas lag or load is high. With a trigger-based tool, throttling can pause the background row copy, but the triggers still fire on every application write, because they are attached to the table. So the migration's load never fully stops, even when the database is struggling. This is the limitation GitHub's gh-ost was designed to remove.

The comparison table in the chapter summarizes: pt-online-schema-change is simple, but triggers add load to every write and cannot be truly paused; Meta OSC is trigger-based and open-sourced.

quiz.q: Why can't a trigger-based OSC tool fully pause when throttled?
quiz.a: Triggers fire on every application write to the original table regardless of throttling, so only the background copy pauses, not the change-capture load.

section: 9.6 Schema and format changes in databases
title: gh-ost: GitHub's triggerless schema change tool
body: gh-ost, from GitHub, captures ongoing changes by reading MySQL's binary log stream, the log of all changes the server replicates, instead of installing triggers. Its README calls triggers 'the source of many limitations and risks'. Being triggerless brings three operational benefits. It can truly pause: when gh-ost throttles, it 'truly ceases writes on master: no row copies and no ongoing events processing'. It can be tested on a replica first. And it offers a controllable cut-over, so operators choose when the swap happens.
deeper:
The chapter's quiz answer summarizes it: gh-ost captures changes by reading the binary log instead of adding triggers, so it can truly pause all its write load when throttled, can be tested on a replica, and gives control over cut-over timing.

True pausing matters most on bad days. If the primary is overloaded or replicas are lagging, gh-ost can stop contributing any load at all, rather than continuing to impose trigger overhead on every write. The migration simply waits and resumes later from the binary log.

Testing on a replica reduces risk before touching the primary: you can run the full migration against a replica, verify the result, and gain confidence in timing and correctness.

Controllable cut-over means the final rename does not have to happen automatically when copying finishes. Operators can postpone it to a quiet time or until they are ready to watch, which is valuable for large, critical tables.

Vitess Online DDL uses a related approach, VReplication, which is also binlog based, and adds integrated scheduling and revertible migrations.

quiz.q: Why is gh-ost called triggerless, and what benefit does that bring?
quiz.a: It reads the binary log instead of adding triggers, so it can truly pause all write load when throttled, be tested on a replica, and control cut-over timing.

section: 9.6 Schema and format changes in databases
title: Vitess Online DDL and Spanner's built-in schema changes
body: Vitess Online DDL captures ongoing changes with VReplication, Vitess's binlog-based replication mechanism, and adds two features beyond standalone tools: integrated scheduling of migrations, and revertible migrations that can be undone after cut-over. Spanner takes a different approach altogether. Schema changes are built into the database and run as background operations across splits, Spanner's units of data partitioning, without locking the table. There is no external ghost-table tool at all; the database itself manages the change safely.
deeper:
The chapter's comparison of online schema change tools shows a progression. Trigger-based tools (pt-online-schema-change, Meta OSC) are simple but impose load on every write and cannot fully pause. Binlog-based tools (gh-ost) remove triggers, can truly pause, and give control over cut-over. Vitess Online DDL builds binlog-based change capture into the database platform itself, so migrations can be scheduled and managed by the system, and adds reversibility.

Revertibility is significant because a schema change that turns out to be wrong after cut-over is otherwise hard to undo, especially if new writes have already landed. A revertible migration keeps a path back, which fits the chapter's persistent theme that every step should be reversible.

Spanner shows the endpoint of the progression: if the database is designed with online schema change as a first-class operation (see Chapter 5), the application and operators do not need a separate tool, and the change runs in the background across all splits. The trade-off is that you depend on the database's own implementation rather than choosing a tool.

quiz.q: What does Vitess Online DDL add beyond gh-ost-style change capture?
quiz.a: Integrated scheduling of migrations and revertible migrations, so a change can be undone after cut-over, on top of binlog-based VReplication.

section: 9.6 Schema and format changes in databases
title: Expand and contract: change schemas one safe step at a time
body: Schema tools change the table, but the application must change too. The safe pattern is expand and contract, also called parallel change. Expand: add the new column or table; nothing reads it yet. Migrate: code writes both old and new, and old rows are backfilled. Switch reads to the new column. Contract: stop writing the old column, then drop it. Every step is backward compatible, so every step can be rolled back. It is a large data migration in miniature.
deeper:
The danger it avoids is a big-bang change where the schema and the code change together. If you rename a column in one step, old application servers still running during a rolling deploy break immediately, and rolling back the code does not restore the old column. Expand and contract separates each change so that at every moment, both the currently running code and the previous version work.

Consider each rollback. After expand, nothing uses the new column, so rolling back means ignoring it. After migrate, both columns are written, so old code reading the old column still works. After switching reads, the old column is still being written, so you can switch reads back. Only contract is hard to undo, which is why it comes last, after the new path has proven itself.

The chapter explicitly calls this the same shape as a large data migration: dual write, backfill, switch reads, then remove the old path. It also matches the two-phase format change for rolling upgrades: first be able to handle the new thing, then start producing it, and only remove the old thing at the end.

quiz.q: Why does expand and contract put dropping the old column last?
quiz.a: It is the one step that cannot easily be rolled back, so it waits until the new column has proven itself; every earlier step remains reversible.

section: 9.7 Storage engine migrations: Meta's InnoDB to MyRocks
title: Meta halved UDB storage by swapping InnoDB for MyRocks
body: A storage engine is the part of a database that stores data on disk (Chapter 5). Changing it under a live database is like changing an engine in a flying plane. Meta did it for its user database, UDB, which was space-bound: it had spare CPU and I/O but was running out of storage. MyRocks, MySQL on top of RocksDB, compresses much better than InnoDB. The migration 'successfully cut our storage usage in half' and finished in 2017, about a year after it started.
deeper:
The motivation is a classic resource-balance argument. If a database cluster is limited by disk capacity while CPU and I/O sit partly idle, then trading some CPU for better compression is a pure win. MyRocks uses RocksDB, an LSM-tree engine, which compresses data more effectively than InnoDB's B-tree layout. Halving storage for a database the size of Meta's UDB is a very large saving in hardware.

The difficulty is that UDB is a live, critical system: user data is read and written constantly, and there is no acceptable window to shut it down, dump everything, and reload. The engine swap also changes performance characteristics, so correctness and behavior have to be verified under real production queries before trusting the new engine.

The chapter's comparison table records it as InnoDB to MyRocks, 2016 to 2017, using replication, shadow queries, and replica-then-primary promotion, with the outcome that storage was cut in half. The next cards cover the five steps and the key principle that made it work: MySQL replication itself was the migration mechanism.

quiz.q: Why was MyRocks a good fit for Meta's UDB?
quiz.a: UDB was space-bound with spare CPU and I/O, and MyRocks compresses much better, trading spare resources for storage; it cut storage usage in half.

section: 9.7 Storage engine migrations: Meta's InnoDB to MyRocks
title: MyRocks step one: add replicas, then verify obsessively
