body: Meta's migration began by adding a MyRocks replica to each replica set, created by dumping data from InnoDB and bulk-loading it into MyRocks, which could transfer hundreds of GB per hour. Then came heavy verification: primary/secondary consistency checks, cross-engine comparison using GTID-consistent snapshots (snapshots taken at the same point in MySQL's global transaction ID sequence), and shadow query testing that replayed production queries on both engines and compared the results. Only after that did MyRocks presence grow.
deeper:
The ordering is deliberate. A MyRocks replica does not serve as the primary and can be discarded at any time, so adding it carries little risk. It becomes a live testbed receiving real replicated writes.

The three verification layers catch different problems. Primary/secondary consistency checks confirm the MyRocks replica stays in sync with its InnoDB primary. Cross-engine comparison with GTID-consistent snapshots compares data at exactly the same logical point in time, so any difference is a real inconsistency rather than a timing artefact. Shadow query testing replays actual production queries against both engines and compares results, catching behavior differences such as query semantics or edge cases that data comparison alone would miss.

The third step grew MyRocks presence by running two MyRocks secondaries next to InnoDB instances. That meant new MyRocks replicas could be copied from MyRocks binary backups rather than reloaded through a full dump and bulk load, which is faster. Throughout these steps, InnoDB remained the primary, so rollback was always as simple as removing MyRocks replicas.

quiz.q: Why did Meta compare engines using GTID-consistent snapshots?
quiz.a: Comparing both engines at the same logical transaction point means any difference is a real inconsistency, not just replication timing.

section: 9.7 Storage engine migrations: Meta's InnoDB to MyRocks
title: Promoting MyRocks to primary was the hardest step
body: After MyRocks replicas were verified and multiplied, Meta promoted MyRocks to primary. Meta's post calls this the hardest part of the migration, because the primary handles all concurrent writes, while replicas only apply a serialized stream of replicated changes. Concurrency exposes behaviors, such as locking and contention, that a replica never sees. After MyRocks proved itself as primary, the final step was removing the InnoDB instances. Only then did the storage savings fully materialize across each replica set.
deeper:
The difference between primary and replica workloads is why verification on replicas, however thorough, cannot remove all risk. A replica receives changes in the order the primary committed them and applies them essentially one after another. A primary receives many independent client writes at once and must handle their concurrency: locking, conflict detection, and scheduling. Bugs or performance problems that only appear under real concurrent load stay hidden until the new engine is actually primary.

This is the same pattern as the source-of-truth flip in large data migrations: the moment the new system becomes authoritative is usually the riskiest. And as with those migrations, Meta still had a way back: InnoDB replicas remained in the replica sets until the final step, so if MyRocks primaries misbehaved, an InnoDB replica could be promoted again.

Removing InnoDB instances came last, after confidence was high, matching the contract step of expand and contract. The whole migration took about a year, finishing in 2017, which reflects how much of the time went into verification rather than copying data.

quiz.q: Why was promoting MyRocks to primary harder than running it as a replica?
quiz.a: The primary handles all concurrent writes, exposing locking and contention behaviors that a replica applying a serialized replication stream never sees.

section: 9.7 Storage engine migrations: Meta's InnoDB to MyRocks
title: The trick: the engine sits below replication
body: The key principle of Meta's InnoDB to MyRocks migration: MySQL replication itself was the migration mechanism. The storage engine sits below the replication layer, so replication does not care which engine stores the data. A MyRocks replica can therefore follow an InnoDB primary, receiving the same stream of changes. You migrate one replica at a time, verify each, promote one eventually, and rollback simply means promoting an InnoDB replica again. No custom dual-write or sync system was needed.
deeper:
The chapter's quiz answer frames it this way: the storage engine sits below replication, a MyRocks replica can replicate from an InnoDB primary, so you can add MyRocks replicas, verify them, promote one, and roll back by promoting an InnoDB replica again.

Compare this with the general large-migration pattern later in the chapter, which requires building dual writes, handling partial failures and ordering, running backfills that must not overwrite newer data, and maintaining reverse writes for rollback. Meta avoided building all of that because MySQL replication already provided a reliable, ordered change stream between instances, and the engine swap happened underneath it.

The broader lesson is to look for an existing layer that is indifferent to the thing you are changing. If the change is below a well-tested abstraction, like engines below replication, the abstraction can carry the migration for you. The same idea explains why the chapter recommends building a data-access abstraction layer before a large migration: it creates a layer above the store where the migration can happen without touching every client.

quiz.q: Why was MySQL replication a natural migration mechanism for InnoDB to MyRocks?
quiz.a: The engine sits below replication, so a MyRocks replica can follow an InnoDB primary; replicas migrate one at a time, and rollback means promoting an InnoDB replica.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Stripe's four-phase recipe for online migrations
body: The biggest operation of all is moving a whole dataset from system A to system B, such as Postgres to a custom sharded store, Cassandra to ScyllaDB, S3 to your own blob store, or on-prem HDFS to cloud object storage. Stripe's 2017 post describes a clean four-phase version. One: dual write to old and new stores, and backfill existing records. Two: change read paths to the new store after verifying consistency. Three: change write paths to write only to the new store. Four: remove old data and code.
deeper:
Stripe's specific tools are worth noting. For backfilling existing records, Stripe used offline MapReduce jobs, which can process large volumes of historical data without going through the live request path. For verifying consistency before switching reads, Stripe used GitHub's Scientist library, which runs both the old and new code paths in production, compares their results, and reports mismatches while still returning the old result to users. That gives real production evidence that the new store returns the same answers.

The order of phases is what makes this safe. While dual writing, the old store stays authoritative, so any problem with the new store is harmless. Reads switch only after verification. Writes stop going to the old store only after reads have proven themselves. Removal of old data and code is last, when there is no longer any reason to go back.

The chapter then expands this into a fuller eight-step pattern, adding pieces that harder real-world migrations needed: an abstraction layer first, explicit verification levels, gradual read shifting, a distinct source-of-truth flip, and a rollback window before decommissioning.

quiz.q: What did Stripe use GitHub's Scientist library for during migrations?
quiz.a: To run reads against both old and new stores in production and compare results, verifying consistency before switching read paths to the new store.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: The eight-step migration pattern, end to end
body: The fuller migration pattern has eight steps. One: build an abstraction layer so all access goes through one data service. Two: dual write, with the old store as source of truth and the new store receiving copies. Three: backfill history into the new store. Four: verify with row counts, checksums, and shadow reads, looping back on mismatches or errors. Five: shift reads gradually, by percentage or cell. Six: flip the source of truth. Seven: keep writing the old store for a rollback window. Eight: stop old writes, archive, decommission.
deeper:
The chapter's key takeaways summarize the same list: abstraction layer, dual write, backfill, verify with shadow reads, shift reads gradually, flip source of truth, keep a rollback window, decommission.

The steps fall into three phases. Steps one through four are preparation: nothing user-facing changes, the old store stays authoritative, and all risk is contained because the new store is only a follower. Steps five and six are the cutover: first reads move, carefully and in slices, then authority itself moves. Steps seven and eight are the tail: keeping a path back until confidence is high, then cleaning up.

The verification step is drawn as a loop in the chapter's diagram. Mismatches or errors send you back to fix dual writes or rerun the backfill, and you only proceed when verification is clean. This is important because it is much cheaper to find a bug at step four than after step six.

The next cards explain each step and what goes wrong at it, drawing on Discord, Netflix, Uber, and Dropbox.

quiz.q: Why does the migration pattern shift reads before flipping the source of truth?
quiz.a: Shifting reads gradually tests the new store with real traffic while the old store is still authoritative, so problems surface before the much riskier authority flip.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Step 1: put one data service in front of the store
body: Before migrating, build an abstraction layer. If 200 services talk directly to Cassandra, a migration means changing 200 services. If they all talk to one data service, you change one. Discord built a Rust data service between its API and database before migrating. Netflix published, in 2024, a key-value data abstraction layer in front of Cassandra and other stores, so backends can change without every application changing. The layer becomes the single place where dual writes and read shifting happen.
deeper:
Uber's 2024 move of its batch data lake to Google Cloud shows the same idea for analytics. It relies on the Hadoop FileSystem interface and on data-access proxies for Presto, Spark, and Hive that federate traffic across on-prem and cloud. Jobs keep using the same interfaces while the proxies decide where each dataset actually lives, so datasets can move one by one without every user changing code.

The abstraction layer pays off in several ways beyond reducing the number of code changes. It is the natural place to implement dual writes, shadow reads, and percentage-based read shifting, since every request passes through it. It lets one team own migration logic instead of coordinating hundreds. It also delivers value independent of the migration: Discord's data services added request coalescing and consistent-hash routing, which reduced load on the database before the migration even started.

This connects to the chapter's opening senior staff lens. Asking 'how do we migrate off it?' at design time often leads straight to this answer: put a service between applications and the store from day one.

quiz.q: Why build an abstraction layer before a large migration?
quiz.a: Clients change once to use it; then dual writes, shadow reads, and read shifting happen in one place instead of in every service that talked to the old store.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Step 2: dual writes break in partial failures and bad ordering
body: In the dual-write step, the application, data service, or a change-data-capture (CDC) stream writes to both old and new stores. Three hard parts. Partial failure: the write to old succeeds but the write to new fails. Ordering: two concurrent updates may reach the new store in a different order than the old. And source of truth: during dual write, the old store stays authoritative and the new store is only a follower. Getting these wrong silently leaves the new store diverged from the old.
deeper:
Each problem has standard fixes. For partial failure, options are retries, a reconciliation job that periodically finds and fixes differences, or writing to the new store asynchronously from a durable log, that is change data capture, instead of in the request path. CDC is attractive because the log persists every change, so a failed write to the new store can simply be retried from the log rather than lost.

For ordering, use versions or timestamps on each record so the new store can reject stale writes. If update A (version 5) arrives after update B (version 6), the new store sees that 5 is older than 6 and ignores it, ending up with the same final state as the old store.

Keeping one source of truth avoids ambiguity. If both stores were treated as authoritative, a disagreement would have no clear resolution. With the old store authoritative, any mismatch is by definition a bug in the new store's copy, which verification can find and fix. Authority moves only at the source-of-truth flip, much later in the pattern.

quiz.q: How does a version or timestamp on each record help dual writes?
quiz.a: Concurrent updates can arrive at the new store out of order; versions let it reject stale writes so it converges to the same state as the old store.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Step 3: backfill history without hurting live data
body: Dual writes only cover new changes, so historical data must be copied into the new store with a backfill. Two rules. It must not overload the old store, which is still serving production; throttle it, and read from replicas or snapshots rather than the primary. And it must not overwrite newer dual-written data: a backfilled row copied from an older snapshot could clobber a fresher version already written by dual writes. Use conditional writes or version checks so older data never replaces newer data.
deeper:
The overwrite problem is easy to miss. Dual writes start first, so by the time the backfill reaches a given row, that row may already have been updated in the new store by live traffic. If the backfill blindly writes the value it read from an older snapshot, it replaces the new, correct value with an old one. The result is silent data loss in the new store, which might only be caught by verification, or not at all.

Conditional writes solve this: the backfill writes a row only if it does not exist yet, or only if its version is newer than what is already there. The same version or timestamp mechanism used to handle ordering in dual writes works here.

The load rule protects production. A backfill copying terabytes can easily saturate the old store's disks or network. Reading from replicas or snapshots moves that load away from the primary, and throttling keeps it bounded. Stripe used offline MapReduce jobs for backfill. Discord, by contrast, found its planned approach too slow and rewrote its migrator in Rust, reaching about 3.2 million messages per second, showing backfill speed can decide a migration's timeline.

quiz.q: How can a backfill corrupt a new store, and how is it prevented?
quiz.a: It may overwrite fresher dual-written rows with older snapshot values; conditional writes or version checks ensure older data never replaces newer data.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Step 4: verify with counts, shadow reads, and edge cases
body: Before any user reads come from the new store, verify it at three levels. Counts and checksums per partition or time range, which quickly show whether whole chunks of data are missing or different. Shadow reads: serve users from the old store, but also read from the new store in the background and compare, logging every mismatch. And sampling of edge cases: deleted items, very large items, and items with unusual encodings, which bulk checks can easily miss. Mismatches send you back to fix and re-verify.
deeper:
Each level catches something the others miss. Counts and checksums are cheap and cover everything, but only tell you that a partition differs, not why, and they only compare stored data, not query behavior. Shadow reads test the real read path with real production queries, catching bugs in how the new store answers queries, such as different sorting, missing filters, or serialization differences, while users remain unaffected because they still get the old store's answer. Stripe did exactly this with GitHub's Scientist library.

Edge case sampling targets where migration bugs hide. Deleted items test whether deletes were propagated through dual writes and not resurrected by backfill. Very large items test size limits and chunking. Unusual encodings test character sets and serialization. These are rare in normal traffic, so shadow reads may seldom hit them.

The chapter's diagram shows verification as a loop: mismatches or errors send the migration back to dual write and backfill fixes. Proceeding with known mismatches just moves them into production after the switch.

quiz.q: What do shadow reads catch that counts and checksums miss?
quiz.a: Differences in how the new store answers real queries, such as ordering, filtering, or serialization, while users still receive the old store's result.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Step 5: shift reads 1, 10, 50, then 100 percent
body: Once verification is clean, start serving users from the new store, gradually. Shift reads 1 percent, then 10 percent, 50 percent, and 100 percent, or move cell by cell. At each step watch latency and error rate before going further. This is canarying applied to data: a small slice of real traffic tests the new store under production conditions, while most users stay on the proven old path. The old store is still the source of truth throughout.
deeper:
Why not switch all reads once verification passes? Because verification tests correctness, not everything else. The new store may be correct but slower under full load, have hot spots only real traffic creates, or fail in ways shadow reads did not exercise because shadow reads were background work whose failures users never saw. Shifting reads gradually exposes those problems while they affect only a small slice of users.

The percentages or cells also make rollback trivial at this stage. Since writes still go to both stores and the old store remains authoritative, moving reads back is just a routing change, with no data consequence.

The cell-by-cell option ties to the chapter's discussion of blast radius. If the system is partitioned into cells by customer or shard, moving reads one cell at a time contains any problem to that cell's users, exactly like deploying code wave by wave. Dropbox's migration to Magic Pocket followed this shape, running a long dark launch with data mirrored before gradually shifting traffic, and passing 90 percent of user data on its own infrastructure months after full launch.

quiz.q: Why shift reads gradually even after verification passes?
quiz.a: Verification tests correctness, not performance under full load or hot spots; small slices expose those issues to few users while rollback is still just routing.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Step 6: the source-of-truth flip is the real cutover
body: Flipping the source of truth is the true cutover: from this moment, the new store is authoritative for reads and writes, and the old store becomes the follower. It is usually the riskiest moment of the whole migration, because mistakes now affect the data users rely on, not just a copy. So the flip is often done per shard or per cell rather than all at once, limiting how much data and how many users any problem at the flip can affect.
deeper:
Before the flip, the new store's problems are recoverable because the old store holds the correct data: re-verify, re-backfill, or rebuild the new store entirely. After the flip, new writes land in the new store first. If it has a bug that loses or corrupts writes, those writes are genuinely at risk unless something else still has them.

That is why the chapter's senior staff lens says rollback is cheap before the source-of-truth flip and very expensive after it, and advises planning the flip for last and doing it in small units. Doing it per shard or per cell means the first flips act as canaries for the flip itself; if something goes wrong, only that shard or cell needs recovery.

Uber's Mezzanine is an interesting contrast: the final switch was done in a single day in September 2014, with no downtime, after dual writes, validation, and backfill. The long preparation is what made a single-day cutover acceptable. Meta's MyRocks migration had the same kind of flip in promoting MyRocks to primary, which Meta called the hardest part.

quiz.q: Why is the source-of-truth flip the riskiest moment of a migration?
quiz.a: Before it, the old store holds correct data so problems are recoverable; after it, new writes depend on the new store, and rollback becomes expensive.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Step 7: keep writing the old store after cutover
body: After the source-of-truth flip, keep a rollback path: continue writing the old store, now as a follower, for some period. If a serious bug appears in the new store, you can flip back, and the old store will already contain every write made since cutover. Without this, 'rollback' means data loss for all writes since cutover, because the old store would be frozen at the moment of the flip. Reverse writes make the flip itself reversible for as long as they run.
deeper:
The chapter's quiz asks why the old store should keep receiving writes after the flip. Answer: writing the old store keeps it current, so if a bug appears you can switch back without losing writes made after the cutover.

This is dual writing in reverse. Before the flip, the old store was authoritative and the new store followed. After it, the roles swap, and the same mechanisms apply: handle partial failures, keep ordering with versions, and keep one clear source of truth.

GitHub's MySQL 5.7 to 8.0 upgrade used exactly this idea: its rollback plan was backward replication from 8.0 to 5.7, so 5.7 servers stayed current and could be returned to service. Even that required work, since collation defaults and roles differed between versions and needed fixes for backward replication to function.

The open question is how long to keep the rollback window. The senior staff lens says: keep reverse writes running until you are sure. Stopping them too early turns any later-discovered bug into a data loss event.

quiz.q: Why should the old store keep receiving writes after the source-of-truth flip?
quiz.a: It stays current, so if a bug appears you can switch back without losing writes made since cutover; otherwise rollback means losing those writes.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Step 8: decommission slowly, and keep backups for months
body: The final migration step is decommissioning the old system: stop writing to it, take a final archive or backup, and delete it. Teams rarely rush this. Many keep the old data read-only for weeks or months, in case a problem surfaces late, like a rarely run report that reveals missing data. Dropbox kept extra backups for six months after moving data to Magic Pocket, 'just in case'. Deletion is irreversible, so it deserves the most caution of any step.
deeper:
Decommissioning is where the chapter's automation principle applies directly: anything irreversible should be slow, guarded, and ideally reviewed. Every earlier step of the migration could be undone. Deleting the old data cannot. Keeping it read-only for a while costs storage, but gives a safety net for bugs that only show up in rare paths: a quarterly job, an old customer account touched once a year, or data with an unusual encoding that verification missed.

The final archive or backup is a second net. Even after the old live system is gone, the archive allows recovering specific records if needed.

This step also connects to the common mistake of declaring a migration done at 100 percent traffic. The last part of decommissioning often uncovers the long tail: a forgotten batch job still reading the old store, a backup system still pointing at old paths, a dataset with odd formats nobody migrated. The chapter's advice is to budget as much time for the last 10 percent as for the first 90. Dropbox's six months of extra backups is a real example of taking that tail seriously.

quiz.q: Why keep old data read-only for weeks or months after a migration?
quiz.a: Deletion is irreversible, and bugs in rare paths may surface late; the old copy and a final archive provide a safety net.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Ask at every step: what's the rollback plan, and for how long?
body: Senior staff lens: the most important design question in a migration is 'what is the rollback plan at each step, and how long does it stay valid?' Rollback is cheap before the source-of-truth flip, when the old store is still authoritative, and very expensive after it, when new writes depend on the new store. So plan the flip for last, do it in small units such as shards or cells, and keep reverse writes to the old store running until you are sure.
deeper:
This lens turns the eight-step pattern into a series of questions. At dual write: rollback is to stop writing the new store. At backfill and verify: rollback is to discard or rebuild the new store. At read shifting: rollback is a routing change. At the flip: rollback requires the old store to be current, which only reverse writes guarantee. After decommissioning: rollback means restoring from an archive, if one exists.

The 'how long does it stay valid' part is crucial. A rollback plan can silently expire. If reverse writes are turned off, or if the old store's schema diverges, or if new features use capabilities only the new store has, the path back closes. Teams should know exactly when each rollback option stops working, and not let it expire by accident.

The real migration stories that follow in the chapter show this lens in practice. GitHub's MySQL upgrade had backward replication from 8.0 to 5.7 as its rollback plan. Meta's MyRocks migration kept InnoDB replicas so an InnoDB primary could be restored. Dropbox kept extra backups for six months. Each team knew what rollback meant at each stage.

quiz.q: Why can a migration rollback plan silently expire?
quiz.a: Turning off reverse writes, diverging schemas, or depending on new-store-only features closes the path back; teams must know when each rollback option stops working.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Uber Mezzanine: Postgres to Schemaless in one day, 2014
body: In 2014 Uber's trip data was growing about 20 percent per month and would exhaust Postgres storage and IOPS by the end of the year. Uber built Schemaless, an append-only store sharded into 4,096 shards on top of MySQL, and migrated in steps under Project Mezzanine. It switched trip IDs from auto-increment integers to UUIDs, rewrote several hundred SQL queries, wrote to both systems and validated, backfilled historical trips, then cut over. The final switch took a single day in September 2014, with no downtime.
deeper:
The ID change illustrates a hidden prerequisite of many migrations. Auto-increment integers are generated by a single database, which does not work across 4,096 independent shards; UUIDs can be generated anywhere without coordination. Changing identifiers touches everything that stores, passes, or indexes them, so it had to happen before the migration itself.

Rewriting several hundred SQL queries reflects the cost of changing data models: Schemaless was not Postgres, so every query had to be expressed against the new store. This is also why an abstraction layer is valuable; without one, those query changes are spread across application code.

The sequence follows the standard pattern: dual write, validate, backfill, cut over. The single-day final switch was possible because all the risk had been worked out in the earlier phases.

Schemaless later evolved into Docstore, which added transactions and Raft-based replication on top of MySQL, described in a 2021 post. The chapter's comparison table records Mezzanine as Postgres to Schemaless in 2014, using dual write, backfill, validate, and a one-day cutover, with no downtime.

quiz.q: Why did Uber switch trip IDs from auto-increment integers to UUIDs before migrating?
quiz.a: Auto-increment IDs come from one database and don't work across 4,096 independent shards; UUIDs can be generated anywhere without coordination.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Dropbox Magic Pocket: months of dark launch before going primary
body: Dropbox started building its own blob store, Magic Pocket, in summer 2013 to move off S3. It ran a dark launch in August 2014, with data mirrored into the new system and ready for production but not yet primary. It launched fully on February 27, 2015, and passed 90 percent of user data on its own infrastructure on October 7, 2015, ahead of its October 30 target. By then the system held over 500 PB. Afterwards, Dropbox kept extra backups for six months 'just in case'.
deeper:
The long dark launch is the lesson the chapter highlights. For months, Magic Pocket ran with real data at real scale before anyone depended on it. That gave Dropbox time to find bugs, tune performance, and build operational confidence in a system that would eventually hold hundreds of petabytes, while S3 remained the safety net.

The timeline also shows how long each phase can take at this scale: about a year from start of building to dark launch, about six months of dark launch before full launch, then about eight more months to move 90 percent of user data. Gradual shifting over many months rather than a one-time switch meant problems would affect a small share of data first.

The six months of extra backups after migration echoes the decommissioning advice: keep a safety net well after traffic has moved, because some problems surface late. The chapter's comparison table summarizes Dropbox Magic Pocket as S3 to own blob store, 2013 to 2015, using a long dark launch, gradual shift, and extra backups, with 90 percent moved by October 2015.

quiz.q: What did Dropbox's long dark launch of Magic Pocket buy it?
quiz.a: Months running with real data at scale before becoming primary, finding bugs and building confidence while S3 remained the safety net.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Discord: 177 Cassandra nodes and trillions of messages
body: By early 2022, Discord's messages cluster had 177 Cassandra nodes storing trillions of messages. Problems included hot partitions (a few partitions receiving far more traffic than others), garbage collection pauses in Cassandra's Java runtime, and compaction backlogs, where background merging of data files falls behind. Before migrating anything, Discord built Rust data services between its API and database, with request coalescing and consistent-hash routing by channel ID. That abstraction layer both reduced load and made the later migration to ScyllaDB possible.
deeper:
Request coalescing means that if many users request the same data at the same time, for example many people opening a busy channel, the data service sends one query to the database and shares the result with all of them. That directly attacks hot partitions, which are exactly the case of many requests for the same data.

Consistent-hash routing by channel ID sends all requests for a given channel to the same data service instance, which makes coalescing effective because concurrent requests for a channel meet in one place.

This is step one of the migration pattern, the abstraction layer, and Discord's story shows it can deliver value on its own. The data services reduced database load immediately, and later they became the single place where migration logic could live, so the API did not need to change.

The problems also explain why a different database was attractive. Garbage collection pauses come from Cassandra's runtime. Compaction backlogs and hot partitions combined to make latency unpredictable. The next card covers the migration to ScyllaDB and its results.

quiz.q: How does request coalescing help with hot partitions?
quiz.a: When many users request the same data at once, the data service sends one database query and shares the result, cutting load on the hot partition.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Discord's 9-day migration: 177 Cassandra nodes to 72 ScyllaDB
body: For the data migration itself, Discord found its planned approach too slow, so it rewrote the data migrator in Rust. The new migrator reached about 3.2 million messages per second and finished the migration in about 9 days. ScyllaDB became primary in May 2022. The results: 72 ScyllaDB nodes instead of 177 Cassandra nodes, historical message p99 latency of 15 ms instead of 40 to 125 ms, and insert p99 latency of 5 ms instead of 5 to 70 ms.
deeper:
The migrator story is a reminder that backfill speed can decide a migration's timeline. Moving trillions of messages at a slow rate could have dragged on for a very long time, keeping the team in the risky mixed state of dual systems. By investing in a faster migrator, Discord compressed the bulk copy into about 9 days.

The latency results are notable for their variability as much as their median. Historical message p99 went from a wide 40 to 125 ms range to 15 ms, and insert p99 from 5 to 70 ms to 5 ms. The old ranges reflect unpredictability caused by problems like garbage collection pauses, compaction backlogs, and hot partitions. Predictable tail latency is often more valuable to users than a better average.

The node count dropping from 177 to 72 is a large operational saving: fewer machines to patch, upgrade, and repair, all the day-2 work this chapter is about. The chapter's comparison table records Discord 2022, Cassandra to ScyllaDB, using a data service layer and a fast bulk migrator, with 177 to 72 nodes as the outcome. Discord published the story in 2023.

quiz.q: Why did Discord rewrite its data migrator before migrating to ScyllaDB?
quiz.a: The planned approach was too slow; the Rust migrator hit about 3.2 million messages per second, finishing in about 9 days instead of prolonging the risky dual-system period.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: GitHub's MySQL 8.0 upgrade: 1,200 hosts, over a year
body: GitHub's move from MySQL 5.7 to 8.0 was a version upgrade, not a system change, but at a scale that made it a migration: 1,200+ hosts, 300+ TB of data, 5.5 million queries per second, 50+ clusters. Preparation began in July 2022 and the process took over a year. Replicas were upgraded in rolling fashion, first taking offline then production traffic. Topology was adjusted so clusters had both 5.7 and 8.0 replication chains, and an 8.0 replica was promoted to primary using Orchestrator.
deeper:
The remaining steps were upgrading internal instances and cleaning up 5.7 hosts after a 24-hour validation period. The overall shape mirrors the MyRocks migration: bring the new version in as replicas, test it with progressively more important traffic, then promote it to primary, keeping the old version around until confidence is high.

Starting replicas on offline traffic, such as analytics or batch jobs, before production traffic is a form of canarying: problems surface on traffic where failure is less costly. Running parallel 5.7 and 8.0 replication chains within the same cluster let both versions stay current, which is essential for being able to go back.

Orchestrator is a MySQL topology management tool used here to perform the primary promotion, the equivalent of the source-of-truth flip, cluster by cluster rather than all at once.

The chapter's comparison table records GitHub 2022 to 2023, MySQL 5.7 to 8.0, using rolling replicas and backward replication rollback, with the outcome that after over a year the fleet was upgraded. The next card covers the rollback plan and the problems found.

quiz.q: Why did GitHub send offline traffic to upgraded replicas before production traffic?
quiz.a: It acts like a canary: problems surface on less critical traffic first, before the new version serves production queries.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: GitHub's MySQL 8.0 rollback plan and the bugs CI missed
body: GitHub's rollback plan for the MySQL 8.0 upgrade was backward replication from 8.0 to 5.7, keeping 5.7 servers current so they could be returned to service. Even that needed fixes, because collation defaults and roles differ between versions. The upgrade also surfaced real problems: a replication applier hang, fixed in MySQL 8.0.28, and queries with huge WHERE IN lists that crashed MySQL in production despite passing CI. Testing had not reproduced production scale.
deeper:
Backward replication is the reverse-writes idea from the migration pattern applied to a version upgrade. Normally, replication flows from older to newer versions without much trouble. Replicating from a newer version to an older one is harder, because the newer version may write things the older does not understand. Collation defaults, which control how text is compared and sorted, changed between 5.7 and 8.0, and roles are a feature that 5.7 handles differently. GitHub had to fix these before the rollback path actually worked. A rollback plan that has never been tested is only a hope.

The WHERE IN crash is a classic example of CI not matching production. Test suites exercise realistic query shapes but rarely the extreme ones: a query with an enormous list of IDs may only appear with real production data. It passed CI and crashed MySQL in production. This is exactly why the upgrade used staged rollout, starting with offline traffic and a subset of replicas, so such problems appeared in contained places.

The replication applier hang shows that even mature database software has bugs at scale, and upgrades are where you find them.

quiz.q: Why did GitHub's backward replication rollback plan need extra work?
quiz.a: Replicating from 8.0 to 5.7 hit differences like collation defaults and roles, which had to be fixed for the rollback path to actually work.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: LinkedIn Venice replaced 500 Voldemort read-only stores
body: LinkedIn built Venice to replace Voldemort's read-only stores for derived data, meaning data computed from other sources, such as outputs of batch jobs, that applications then read. By 2018, about 500 Voldemort read-only deployments had been fully migrated to Venice. Venice uses Helix, a cluster management framework, for replica placement and rolling restarts. The chapter's comparison table describes the technique as full-push replacement, with about 500 deployments migrated as the published outcome.
deeper:
Derived data has a property that simplifies migration: it can be regenerated. Because it is computed from other sources, a new store can be populated by pushing a full dataset into it, rather than carefully syncing a live, authoritative dataset with dual writes. This is what full-push replacement refers to: the new system receives complete datasets and takes over serving them, rather than following a live source of truth.

The scale here is in the number of deployments rather than the size of a single dataset. Migrating about 500 separate deployments requires repeatable, largely automated process; each one individually might be modest, but doing them one by one by hand would be impractical.

The use of Helix for replica placement and rolling restarts connects Venice to the chapter's earlier themes. Rolling restarts are how upgrades happen without downtime, and placement determines durability and failure-domain spread. By building on a framework designed for this, Venice gets the day-2 operational capabilities that the chapter argues must be part of any storage design from the start.

quiz.q: Why can derived data use full-push replacement instead of dual writes?
quiz.a: Derived data is computed from other sources, so the new store can be filled by pushing complete datasets rather than syncing a live authoritative copy.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Uber's exabyte-scale move from Hadoop to Google Cloud
body: Announced in 2024, Uber is moving batch analytics and ML training from on-prem Hadoop, with more than 1 exabyte of data across tens of thousands of servers in each of two regions, to Google Cloud Storage. Two key techniques: a mapping between HDFS paths and cloud buckets with IAM policies, and proxies that let Presto, Spark, and Hive jobs run against either location. Together they let the migration happen dataset by dataset without every user changing code.
deeper:
At this scale, a big-bang migration is impossible. The data cannot be copied in one go, and the users, thousands of analytics and ML jobs, cannot all be changed at once. The solution is to make location invisible to users.

The path mapping translates the familiar HDFS paths jobs already use into cloud bucket locations, with IAM (identity and access management) policies preserving who can access what. The proxies federate traffic: when a Presto, Spark, or Hive job reads a path, the proxy decides whether that dataset currently lives on-prem or in the cloud and routes accordingly. Uber also relies on the Hadoop FileSystem interface, the standard abstraction these engines already use for storage.

This is the abstraction layer step of the migration pattern applied to a batch data lake. Once in place, each dataset can move independently: copy, verify, update the mapping, and jobs follow automatically. Moving dataset by dataset also naturally limits blast radius.

The chapter's comparison table records Uber GCP as 2024 onward, HDFS to GCS, using path mapping and federating proxies, with the outcome listed as in progress, as announced.

quiz.q: How do Uber's proxies let the data lake migrate dataset by dataset?
quiz.a: Jobs keep using the same paths; proxies route each read to on-prem or cloud based on where that dataset currently lives, so no user code changes.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: Seven real migrations, one shared playbook
body: The chapter's comparison of real migrations: Uber Mezzanine (2014, Postgres to Schemaless, one-day cutover, no downtime). Dropbox Magic Pocket (2013 to 2015, S3 to own blob store, long dark launch, 90 percent moved by October 2015). Meta MyRocks (2016 to 2017, storage cut in half). Discord (2022, Cassandra to ScyllaDB, 177 to 72 nodes). GitHub (2022 to 2023, MySQL 5.7 to 8.0, over a year). LinkedIn Venice (by 2018, about 500 deployments). Uber GCP (2024 onward, HDFS to GCS, in progress).
deeper:
The key techniques differ in detail: dual write, backfill, and validation at Uber Mezzanine; a long dark launch, gradual shift, and extra backups at Dropbox; replication, shadow queries, and replica-then-primary promotion at Meta; a data service layer and fast bulk migrator at Discord; rolling replicas and backward replication rollback at GitHub; full-push replacement at LinkedIn; path mapping and federating proxies at Uber GCP.

But the chapter's key takeaways point out that these migrations share the same lessons: long validation phases, small cutover units, and a real rollback path. Every successful story spent more time proving the new system than copying data. Every one moved authority in pieces, whether by shard, replica set, cluster, deployment, or dataset. And every one kept a path back: backward replication, InnoDB replicas, reverse writes, or months of extra backups.

Notice also how often an abstraction layer appears: Discord's data services, Uber's proxies, MySQL replication at Meta. Where one existed or was built first, the migration itself became much simpler. Timelines are long too: about a year for Meta, over a year for GitHub, two-plus years for Dropbox.

quiz.q: What three lessons do all the chapter's real migrations share?
quiz.a: Long validation phases, small cutover units, and a real rollback path.

section: 9.8 Large data migrations in depth
title: 100 percent of traffic moved doesn't mean the migration is done
body: Common mistake: declaring the migration done when traffic is 100 percent on the new system. The long tail is where the risk is: the last 1 percent of datasets with odd formats, the forgotten batch job still reading the old store, the backup system still pointing at old paths. If the old system is shut down while these remain, things break or data is silently lost. The chapter's advice: budget as much time for the last 10 percent as for the first 90.
deeper:
The chapter's quiz asks for reasons the last 10 percent often takes as long as the first 90. Its examples: rare data formats and edge cases, forgotten readers or batch jobs, backup and disaster-recovery paths still pointing at the old store, owners who are hard to find, and stricter verification needed before deleting the old data.

Each reflects why the tail is hard. The first 90 percent is the common case, handled by the main migration tooling. The tail is everything the tooling did not anticipate. Forgotten consumers are particularly dangerous because nobody knows to check them: a monthly report or a disaster recovery job may run rarely and only fail when the old store disappears. Backup systems pointing at old paths are worse, because the failure is silent until you need a restore. Finding owners of odd datasets takes human coordination, which is slow.

The final step, deleting old data, is irreversible and therefore deserves the strictest verification. That extra care takes time too. Dropbox's six months of extra backups and the practice of keeping old data read-only for weeks or months both reflect respect for this tail.

quiz.q: Give two reasons the last 10 percent of a migration takes as long as the first 90.
quiz.a: Rare formats and edge cases the tooling missed, and forgotten readers, batch jobs, or backup paths still pointing at the old store; also hard-to-find owners and stricter pre-deletion verification.

section: 9.9 Hardware refresh and datacenter decommissioning
title: Retiring a rack: drain, evacuate, verify, wait, wipe
body: Hardware ages out, and new generations bring denser drives and more efficient servers, so fleets refresh continuously. Decommissioning a rack or cluster follows five steps. Mark it draining, so no new data is placed there. Evacuate every chunk, shard, and replica elsewhere, rate-limited. Verify with a program that nothing still has its only copy or a needed fragment on the draining hardware. Power off, then wait, keeping the disks for a safety window. Finally, securely wipe or physically destroy the drives.
deeper:
The verification step has a specific requirement: it must use the actual metadata, not assumptions. It is easy to assume evacuation worked because the evacuation tool reported success, or because the rack 'should' be empty according to a plan. The only reliable check is to query the system's real placement metadata and confirm, for every chunk and stripe, that enough copies or fragments exist elsewhere. A single missed chunk with its last copy on the rack becomes permanent data loss when the rack is wiped.

Powering off and waiting before wiping adds a second layer of protection. If verification missed something, the disks can be powered back on and the data recovered. Only after the safety window passes do the drives get securely erased or physically destroyed before leaving the facility, which is a security requirement covered in Chapter 11.

Rate-limiting evacuation matters because moving a rack's worth of data competes with user traffic and repair, the same bandwidth trade-off as disk repair. Chapter 8 covers the capacity side of hardware refresh, such as planning when to buy and retire.

quiz.q: Why must decommissioning verification use actual metadata, not assumptions?
quiz.a: Tool reports or plans can be wrong; only real placement metadata confirms no chunk still has its only copy on the hardware about to be wiped.

section: 9.9 Hardware refresh and datacenter decommissioning
title: Shutting down a datacenter: the hard part is finding everything
body: Decommissioning a whole datacenter uses the same drain, evacuate, verify, wait, and wipe idea as a rack, at a larger scale, plus network, DNS, and dependency cleanup. The hardest part is usually finding everything: forgotten services with hardcoded addresses, backups stored locally, and test systems nobody owns. Any of these can break or lose data when the datacenter goes dark. The S3 2017 incident is also a warning here: operations that remove capacity must be slow and have minimum-capacity guards.
deeper:
The discovery problem is the datacenter-scale version of a migration's long tail. Well-known production services are easy to move because their owners are active and their dependencies are documented. The dangerous leftovers are the things nobody remembers. A service with a hardcoded IP address in the datacenter will start failing when that address disappears. A backup stored on local disks in the datacenter will be destroyed along with it, and nobody will notice until a restore is needed. A test system with no owner might actually be quietly used by something important.

Network and DNS cleanup is required because datacenters have their own address ranges and name records, and stale entries can route traffic into a void.

The S3 link is about the removal action itself. Decommissioning is an operation that removes capacity, the same category as the command that caused the 2017 outage. AWS's remediation, remove capacity slowly, with safeguards against going below minimum capacity, applies directly: decommissioning tooling should move slowly and refuse to remove capacity that would leave the system short.

quiz.q: Why is finding everything the hardest part of decommissioning a datacenter?
quiz.a: Forgotten services with hardcoded addresses, local-only backups, and ownerless test systems can break or lose data when it shuts down, and nobody knows to check them.

section: 9.10 Observability for storage
title: Six levels of storage signals, from disk to deploys
body: You cannot operate what you cannot see, so storage needs signals at six levels. Device: SMART counters, media errors, per-disk latency histograms, for early drain of failing or slow disks. Node: disk utilization, queue depth, CPU, NIC saturation, compaction backlog, to find hot nodes and noisy neighbors. Data: degraded chunks, repair queue, scrub progress, checksum mismatches, showing durability risk. Service: request rate, errors, latency per tenant. Capacity: growth and days until full. Change: current versions, configs, and recent deploys.
deeper:
Each level answers a different operational question. Device signals feed proactive draining, including reallocated sectors and temperature alongside latency histograms. Node signals find hot nodes and noisy neighbors, where one tenant's heavy workload hurts others sharing hardware; compaction backlog is included because a node falling behind on background work will degrade soon.

The data level, covering degraded chunk count, chunks at minimum redundancy, repair queue size and rate, scrub progress, and checksum mismatches, is called the most important dashboard, because it directly measures durability risk. Service signals measure user experience against SLOs, with latency at p50, p99, and p99.9 broken down per tenant and operation so one customer's problem is not averaged away.

Capacity signals, meaning used, free, growth rate, and days until full per cluster, exist so hardware can be ordered in time, since procurement takes a long time. Change signals, current versions and configs per cell plus recent deploys, let you correlate incidents with changes. Given that most incidents are triggered by binary or config pushes, 'what changed recently?' is often the fastest route to the cause.

quiz.q: Why track current versions, configs, and recent deploys as observability signals?
quiz.a: Most incidents are triggered by binary or config pushes, so correlating an incident with recent changes is often the fastest way to find its cause.

section: 9.10 Observability for storage
title: A 5 ms average can hide a 2-second p99.9
body: Use histograms, not averages. An average latency of 5 ms can hide a p99.9 of 2 seconds, meaning one request in a thousand takes 2 seconds while the average still looks healthy. At high fan-out, where one user request touches many disks or servers, the slowest participant decides user latency (Chapter 8). So record full latency histograms per disk and per node. That is how you find the one slow disk that makes every erasure-coded read touching it slow.
deeper:
Averages hide exactly the problems that matter most in storage. A slow disk might add hundreds of milliseconds to a small fraction of reads, barely moving the average for the node, but every request that includes that disk suffers. With erasure coding, a read may need fragments from several disks at once, so the probability that at least one of them is the slow disk grows with fan-out. The tail of one component becomes the typical experience for users.

Histograms preserve the whole distribution, so you can see p99 and p99.9 and compare individual disks. Keeping them per disk, not only aggregated per node or cluster, is what lets you find the specific outlier. Once found, the slow disk can be drained proactively, which connects back to the detection step of the repair loop, where rising latency is treated as a sign of failure.

The service-level observability signals follow the same principle: latency at p50, p99, and p99.9 per tenant and operation, rather than one average. The chapter's key takeaways state it directly: observability must include latency histograms, not just averages.

quiz.q: Why keep latency histograms per disk rather than one average per node?
quiz.a: An average hides tails; at high fan-out one slow disk slows every read that touches it, and only per-disk histograms reveal which disk to drain.

section: 9.10 Observability for storage
title: Durability problems are silent until the data is gone
body: Availability problems are loud: users notice errors and complain. Durability problems are silent until data is gone. So storage teams must watch durability directly. The dashboard that matters most asks: how many chunks are at their last unit of redundancy right now, and how fast is repair going? Continuous scrubbing, background reading and checksum verification of stored data (Chapter 10), finds silent corruption before a later failure makes it permanent by destroying the only good copy.
deeper:
The asymmetry drives priorities. If you only monitor what users feel, you will see outages but miss the slowly accumulating conditions that cause data loss: a growing number of chunks at minimum redundancy, repair falling behind, or corrupted copies nobody has read in months. All of these are invisible to users until the moment a further failure turns risk into loss.

The last-unit-of-redundancy count is the most direct measure of how close the system is to losing data. Paired with repair rate, it tells you whether that risk is shrinking or growing. This is also what the chapter recommends alerting on: durability risk, such as data at minimum redundancy or repair falling behind, alongside user-visible symptoms.

Scrubbing covers a gap that repair cannot see. Repair responds to known failures, like a dead disk. Silent corruption, where a disk returns wrong data without reporting an error, is not a known failure until someone reads the data and checks it. Scrubbing reads everything periodically and verifies checksums, so a corrupted copy can be repaired from a good one while good copies still exist.

quiz.q: Why does storage need scrubbing in addition to repair?
quiz.a: Repair only reacts to known failures; scrubbing reads data and verifies checksums to find silent corruption while good copies still exist to repair from.

section: 9.11 Runbooks, on-call, and automation vs humans
title: Good runbooks are short, tested, and become automation
body: A runbook is a documented procedure for a known situation, such as 'disk failed', 'node unreachable', 'repair queue growing', or 'cluster 85 percent full'. Good runbooks are short, tested, and linked directly from the alert itself, so the on-call engineer reaches the right procedure instantly instead of searching a wiki at 3am. The best runbooks are gradually turned into automation: once a procedure is well understood and reliably correct, a program can run it faster and more consistently than a person.
deeper:
Each property addresses a real failure mode. Short, because someone responding to an alert under pressure will skip or misread a long document. Tested, because a runbook that has never been executed may contain wrong commands or outdated steps, and the first time you learn that should not be during an incident. Linked from the alert, because the moments spent finding documentation are moments the system stays broken.

The progression from runbook to automation is a natural lifecycle. A new kind of problem is first handled by humans, who write down what worked. Repeated use refines the runbook into something precise. At that point it is effectively a program written in English, and translating it to code removes human error and delay. At fleet scale this is necessary: disk failures happen about 13 times per day in a Backblaze-sized fleet, far too often for humans to follow a manual procedure each time.

The automation versus human table later in the section shows the endpoint: well-understood events like single disk failures are fully automatic, while novel failures remain human-led with a runbook and incident process.

quiz.q: Why should runbooks be linked from the alert itself?
quiz.a: So the on-call engineer reaches the right procedure instantly under pressure, instead of losing time searching documentation while the system stays broken.

section: 9.11 Runbooks, on-call, and automation vs humans
title: Don't page a human for every dead disk
body: Good storage alerting pages on two things: user-visible symptoms, such as errors and latency SLO burn (using up the error budget faster than allowed), and durability risk, such as data at minimum redundancy or repair falling behind. It does not page for individual disk failures at scale. At about 13 failures per day in a Backblaze-sized fleet, paging per disk burns people out and buries real problems in noise. Disk failures are handled by automation and a daily replacement ticket queue.
deeper:
The chapter's quiz makes the arithmetic explicit: 300,000 drives at 1.5 percent AFR is about 4,500 failures per year, about 12 per day. Per-disk paging would be constant noise, so disk failures should be handled by automation and a replacement ticket queue, with pages only for durability risk or user-visible symptoms.

The principle is that a page should mean a human needs to act now. A single disk failure does not need that: the repair loop automatically rebuilds the lost copies, and the physical swap can wait for a routine ticket. What does need immediate attention is when automation is not coping: many chunks at minimum redundancy, repair falling behind, or users seeing errors.

Alert fatigue is a real reliability risk. If engineers are paged a dozen times a day for things that resolve themselves, they learn to ignore pages, and the one page that matters gets missed or delayed. Paging on durability risk rather than on individual failures also catches the dangerous combinations, such as a second failure during a rebuild, which a per-disk page would not distinguish from a routine failure.

quiz.q: Why page on durability risk rather than individual disk failures?
quiz.a: Single failures are routine and handled by automation; paging per disk causes alert fatigue, while durability-risk alerts fire only when automation isn't coping.

section: 9.11 Runbooks, on-call, and automation vs humans
title: Automation scales operations, and scales disasters too
body: At fleet scale most operations must be automated: disk replacement workflows, repair, rebalancing, rolling upgrades, and drains. Humans cannot keep up with hundreds of events per day. But automation can also cause disasters faster than humans. Both famous outages, S3 in 2017 and Meta in 2021, involved tools that executed destructive operations at scale. Mature teams therefore match each operation type with a default mode, from fully automatic to human-led, and a guardrail that limits damage if something goes wrong.
deeper:
The chapter's table maps operations to modes and guardrails. Single disk failure and repair: fully automatic, guarded by rate limits and risk-based priority. Rolling upgrades and firmware: automatic with staged waves, guarded by canary analysis, auto-rollback, and a redundancy budget. Draining a rack: automatic after human approval, guarded by verifying no sole copies remain and slow evacuation. Removing a cluster or deleting data: human approval and two-person review, guarded by minimum-capacity checks and a delay before real deletion. Unknown or novel failure: human-led, supported by a runbook and incident process.

The pattern is that human involvement increases with how destructive and how unfamiliar the operation is. Routine, reversible, well-understood operations run without humans because humans would only slow them down and add error. Destructive or novel ones get human judgment, but even then, guardrails in the tools limit the damage a wrong decision can cause.

Notice that every mode has a guardrail, including fully automatic ones. Automation without limits is how a small bug or wrong input becomes a fleet-wide outage in seconds.

quiz.q: Why does removing a cluster require two-person review while disk repair is fully automatic?
quiz.a: Disk repair is routine and reversible; removing a cluster or deleting data is destructive and irreversible, so it needs human judgment plus minimum-capacity checks and a deletion delay.

section: 9.11 Runbooks, on-call, and automation vs humans
title: Automate the reversible fast; make the irreversible slow
body: A useful rule: automation should be allowed to do anything that is reversible, quickly. Anything irreversible should be slow, guarded, and ideally reviewed. Deleting data, removing capacity below a threshold, and changing placement rules for durability fall in the irreversible class. The decision flow: for any event or planned change, ask whether it is reversible and well understood. If yes, automation executes with rate limits. If no, require human approval, apply tool guardrails like minimum capacity and blast radius checks, and execute slowly, staged by cell.
deeper:
Both paths then converge on monitoring: watch SLOs and durability signals, and on any anomaly, pause and roll back. So even reversible, automated operations are not fire-and-forget; they stop themselves if something looks wrong.

The reversible/irreversible split explains why the rule works. A reversible operation that goes wrong can be undone, so the cost of a mistake is bounded and speed is valuable. An irreversible operation that goes wrong cannot be undone, so the only protection is catching the mistake before it completes. Slowness is itself a safety mechanism: it gives monitoring and humans time to notice and stop the operation partway.

Placement rule changes being listed as irreversible may seem surprising, since a config can be changed back. But a placement change can cause data movement and, if wrong, leave data under-protected; if failures hit during that window, the resulting data loss cannot be reversed. The chapter's key takeaways summarize the principle: automate reversible operations fully, and make irreversible ones slow, guarded, and reviewed.

quiz.q: Why is slowness itself a safety mechanism for irreversible operations?
quiz.a: Since the result cannot be undone, the only protection is stopping a mistake partway; slow execution gives monitoring and humans time to notice and halt it.

section: 9.11 Runbooks, on-call, and automation vs humans
title: Ask every tool: what's the worst a wrong input can do?
body: Senior staff lens: ask of every operational tool, 'What is the worst thing this command can do if the input is wrong?' If the answer is 'remove a region's capacity' or 'delete a cluster's data', the tool needs three things: a hard ceiling on how much it can affect, a slow mode so damage accumulates gradually rather than instantly, and a second check before it proceeds. The S3 2017 remediation, remove capacity slowly and never below minimum, is a template worth copying.
deeper:
The question shifts attention from the intended use of a tool to its worst-case misuse. Most tools are designed and tested for the correct input. But the S3 outage happened because an input was wrong, and the tool faithfully did what it was told at full speed. Asking what a wrong input could do forces you to design for the typo, the wrong cluster name, or the extra zero.

Each safeguard addresses a different part of the risk. A hard ceiling bounds the maximum damage no matter what the input says. A slow mode means that even within the ceiling, damage unfolds over time, so monitoring and humans can intervene, matching the chapter's rule that irreversible operations should be slow. A second check, such as another engineer's review or an automated invariant validator, catches the wrong input before execution.

This lens ties together the chapter's threads: change causes most outages, config and commands are as dangerous as code, and irreversible actions deserve guardrails. The Meta 2021 outage adds a warning: the audit tool meant to be that second check had a bug, so safety checks themselves need testing.

quiz.q: What three safeguards should a tool have if a wrong input could delete a cluster's data?
quiz.a: A hard ceiling on how much it can affect, a slow mode so damage unfolds gradually, and a second check before it proceeds.

section: Key takeaways
title: Chapter 9 in one card: change safely, forever
body: Failures and planned changes are continuous: Meta found upgrades about 1,000 times more frequent than failures, and Google says most incidents come from pushes. Repair must be fast, risk-prioritized, and widely spread; erasure coding multiplies its traffic. SMART cannot predict most failures. Zero-downtime upgrades need two-way compatibility, graceful handoff, and a redundancy budget. Canaries detect, cells contain, and config deserves the same pipeline as code. Migrations need an abstraction layer, dual writes, verification, gradual cutover, and rollback. Automate the reversible; guard the irreversible.
deeper:
The remaining takeaways fill in the details. Online schema change tools such as pt-osc, gh-ost, and Vitess copy into a ghost table, capture changes, throttle, and cut over, while application changes use expand and contract. The full migration sequence is abstraction layer, dual write, backfill, verify with shadow reads, shift reads gradually, flip source of truth, keep a rollback window, decommission. Real migrations at Uber, Dropbox, Meta, Discord, GitHub, and LinkedIn share the same lessons: long validation phases, small cutover units, and a real rollback path.

Observability for storage must include durability signals, such as data at minimum redundancy and repair rate, and latency histograms rather than averages. Google found over 36 percent of failed drives showed no SMART signal at all, which is why redundancy and repair, not prediction, are the foundation.

The unifying idea is that every change should be reversible, contained, and observed. When a step cannot be reversed, like deleting data or removing capacity, it should be slow, guarded, and reviewed. That is the answer to the chapter's central question of how to change a system constantly without breaking it.

quiz.q: What single idea ties together the chapter's techniques?
quiz.a: Every change should be reversible, contained, and observed; steps that cannot be reversed must be slow, guarded, and reviewed.
